00_start_here.content:
START HERE: St. Mary’s Virtual Residency
What this is
A residency you run yourself. It follows the four ASHP PGY1 competency areas (patient care, practice advancement, leadership, teaching) and is built around what St. Mary’s actually sees: trauma, stroke, NICU, PICU, Labor & Delivery, adult critical care and the IV room.
How to pick back up in a new chat
Open a new chat in the RxCareer-Agent project and paste:

Open my St. Mary’s Virtual Residency folder (Documents/St Marys Virtual Residency). Read CLAUDE.md, index.md and the last entries in log.md, then continue with the next module in the 12 week plan.

Folder map

CLAUDE.md: the rules Claude follows in this folder.
index.md: every page, one line each.
log.md: what was added and when.
raw/: drop anything here (guideline PDFs, St. Mary’s policies, order sets, your own notes, Pyrls PDFs). Claude reads it and updates the wiki.
wiki/curriculum/: the 12 week plan and daily routine.
wiki/st-marys/: how leadership thinks, service lines.
wiki/sources/: where to stay current, and how to use Pyrls.
wiki/clinical/: the modules.
wiki/cases/: practice cases with model answers.

Best way to use Obsidian
Open this folder as a vault in Obsidian. The links become clickable, and the graph view shows how topics connect.
Your three habits

Daily (20 min): one case from wiki/cases/, out loud, timed.
Weekly (2 hours): one module from the plan, plus one ISMP alert and one new FDA safety communication.
Every shift: write down one question you couldn’t answer in 30 seconds. Drop it in raw/questions.md. Claude turns it into a wiki page.

app_build_spec.title: APP_BUILD_SPEC
app_build_spec.content:
App Build Spec: St. Mary’s Virtual Residency (private web app)
Status: planned 2026-10-17. Read this with CLAUDE.md before building anything.
1. The core idea
The Obsidian folder is the app. One set of markdown files, three ways to use it:

Edit in Obsidian on the Mac.
Store in a private GitHub repo (history, backups, review of every change).
Publish as a private website on Cloudflare Pages, locked with Cloudflare Access so only her email can log in.

No database, no custom backend. Markdown in, website out.
2. Stack (simplest that works)








































NeedToolWhySite generatorQuartz v4 (quartz.jzhao.xyz)Built for Obsidian vaults: wikilinks, backlinks, graph view, full text search, callouts, all built inQuick findQuartz built in searchSearches every page and heading; no extra codeHostingCloudflare PagesFree; deploys on every GitHub pushPrivacyCloudflare Access (Zero Trust, free tier)Login by one time code to her email onlySync Obsidian to GitHubObsidian Git plugin, or GitHub DesktopPush changes with one clickMonthly updatesScheduled Claude task (see section 6)Opens a pull request; she approves before anything goes live
Skipped on purpose: custom app, user accounts, database, scoring backend. Add later only if a real need shows up (see section 8).
3. Repo layout
/content
  index.md                 home: modules, latest changes, quick links
  whats-new/               one page per month (2026-11.md ...)
  curriculum/
  clinical/                one page per module
  cases/                   one file per case
  sources/registry.md      every source with an ID
  quick-find/              one line answer pages (doses, antidotes, targets)
/raw                       NOT published (see privacy rules)
CLAUDE.md, APP_BUILD_SPEC.md, log.md

4. Every claim traceable (Pharmacy Decoder style)
Source registry (sources/registry.md), one entry per source:
### SRC-ACOG-CO767-2019
- Title: ACOG Committee Opinion 767, Emergent Therapy for Acute Onset Severe Hypertension
- Year: 2019 (reaffirmed: [date])
- Public link: https://...
- Pyrls link: app.pyrls.com/... (opens with her Pyrls login)
- DOI or PMID:
- Last verified: 2026-10-17
- Superseded by: (blank unless replaced)

In the pages, every dose or threshold gets a footnote pointing to the registry:
Magnesium sulfate 4 to 6 g IV load, then 1 to 2 g/h.[^acog222]
[^acog222]: [[registry#SRC-ACOG-PB222-2020]] · section "Seizure prophylaxis"

Quartz renders footnotes as hover previews, so each claim is one click from its source.
Source order: the original source comes first (guideline, trial, FDA label, ISMP page) so a colleague without Pyrls can open it. Pyrls is the second link. When Pyrls cites an original source, record that original in the registry too.
Rule: a claim with no footnote is marked [VERIFY] and listed on a “Needs source” page that builds itself from search.
5. Cases (realistic, overlapping)
One file per case with frontmatter:
---
id: CASE-OB-TRAUMA-001
modules: [LD_Obstetrics_Core, Trauma_Core, Anticoagulation_Core]
difficulty: 3        # 1 intern, 2 staff, 3 resident, 4 specialist
setting: ED trauma bay, 02:00
tags: [pregnancy, TXA, reversal, Rh immune globulin]
---

Body:

Scenario (labs, vitals, home meds, the order you’re asked to verify).
Questions in order, the way it unfolds on a shift (3 to 6 per case).
Answer in a collapsed callout so it stays hidden until clicked:
> [!answer]- Model answer … > [!protocol]- Clinical breakdown (the step by step pharmacist workup, the sources, what to monitor, what to say on the phone).
Links to every module it touches, so backlinks show “cases that use this page.”

Overlap cases on purpose, because that’s how the hospital works. For example: pregnant trauma patient on enoxaparin; neonate whose mother got magnesium and an incomplete GBS course; stroke patient on apixaban who needs thrombectomy; PICU DKA patient with hypokalemia and cerebral edema.
Target: 10 cases per module (about 120), plus 20 overlap cases, built 8 to 10 per session.
6. Monthly update system
A scheduled Claude task on the 1st of every month:

Check each feed: FDA Drug Safety Communications and new approvals, ISMP Acute Care alerts, ASHP drug shortages, and AHA/ASA, ACOG, AAP, IDSA, SCCM, EAST, CHEST, ADA guideline pages.
For anything new, find the affected pages using the source registry (“which pages cite SRC-X?”).
Write whats-new/YYYY-MM.md: what changed, why it matters at St. Mary’s, the links, and the pages affected.
Propose page edits in a pull request on GitHub. Nothing changes the live site until she reviews and merges (clinical accuracy gate).
Update “Last verified” dates and run the lint (missing sources, superseded guidelines, broken links).

The home page shows the latest “What’s New” at the top.
7. Privacy rules (must follow)

No patient information anywhere, ever, including in the private site.
St. Mary’s internal documents (order sets, policies, protocols) stay in /raw/stmarys/ on her Mac only. That folder is in .gitignore and never goes to GitHub or Cloudflare. Wiki pages can say “St. Mary’s protocol: check order set X” without copying it.
Pyrls: links only, no pasted content (copyright). The links work only when she’s logged in, which is fine for a private site.
Cloudflare Access policy: allow only her email.

8. Phases








































PhaseWhatDone when1Private GitHub repo from this folder; Quartz installed; Cloudflare Pages + AccessShe can open the private URL on her phone2Source registry; retrofit footnotes into Modules 1 to 6Every dose has a clickable source3Modules 7 to 12 (anticoagulation, ID, critical care, IV room, med safety, project)All 12 built4Case bank to about 140 using the case formatAll modules have 10 cases5Monthly scheduled task liveFirst “What’s New” page publishedLater, only if neededQuiz scoring or spaced repetition (for example export cases to Anki), mobile app wrapperShe asks for it
9. Other tools (link, don’t merge)
Her MTM Clinical Workbench and CMR Command Center (in ~/hunter_holistic_app/Outcomes/Hunter_Holistic_MTM_Lab_Obsidian_Vault/) stay separate apps, because they serve her MTM contract work, not hospital practice. If wanted later: publish each as its own private Cloudflare site under the same Access login and add a small “My tools” link list on the home page. Never copy their content into this residency.
10. Interview question bank
The clinical, IV room and order verification questions in raw/interview_prep (05, 05b, 05c, 06, plus the clinical parts of 04 and 11) become cases in the case format. Skip the personal and story files (02, 02b, 03, 07, 09, 10).
11. Journal club library

Template: wiki/journal-club/Journal_Club_Template.md (JAMA Users’ Guides, RoB 2 domains, CONSORT 2025).
One page per trial, tagged to modules (for example CRASH-2 to Trauma_Core). Bottom line first.

12. Drug information hub (her own references)
Build her own reference pages, organized the way hospital drug references are organized, but with her own names and her own content from public, citable sources. Do not copy content, screenshots, layouts or names from Lexicomp, Micromedex, Trissel’s or Sanford (copyright and trademark).



































Her sectionModeled on the role ofPublic sources to build fromDrug Monographsgeneral drug reference (Lexicomp or Micromedex type)FDA label via DailyMed, openFDA, guidelinesIV Compatibility and AdminIV compatibility reference (Trissel’s type)FDA labels (dilution, stability, Y site statements), published studies; every page says “confirm in the hospital’s IV compatibility database”Antimicrobial Guideantimicrobial therapy guide (Sanford type)IDSA, AAP Red Book public summaries, CDCLiteraturePubMedLinks onlySimulations: each case names which type of reference a pharmacist would open first and why, then gives the answer and the source.
13. Handoff
New chat prompt: “Open my St. Mary’s Virtual Residency folder. Read CLAUDE.md, APP_BUILD_SPEC.md, index.md and the end of log.md. Continue with the next phase.”

cases/cases_anticoag_and_verification.title: Cases_Anticoag_and_Verification
cases/cases_anticoag_and_verification.content:
Practice Cases: Anticoagulation and Order Verification
All cases are invented for teaching. Built from the clinical interview questions, with updated numbers. 60 seconds each, out loud. Top 10% = answer + source and year + exact order + monitoring.
Key: ✅✅ two independent sources · ✅ one source · ⚠️ [VERIFY]
Study pages: Anticoagulation_Core · Heparin · Enoxaparin · 4F_PCC · Insulin_IV_DKA · Potassium_Chloride_IV

Case 1 (Anticoag + surgery): Apixaban before a hip replacement
An 82 year old, 58 kg, SCr 1.1, takes apixaban 5 mg BID for atrial fibrillation. Elective hip replacement in 4 days. The surgeon asks when to stop it and whether to bridge.
Model answer: “Two catches. First, she meets 2 of 3 dose reduction criteria (age 80 or older, weight 60 kg or less), so her AF dose should be 2.5 mg BID. Second, a hip replacement is high bleed risk, so per PAUSE she skips 2 days before surgery and the day of surgery: last dose 3 days before. No bridging for a DOAC. Restart 48 to 72 hours after surgery once bleeding is controlled (CHEST 2022).”
Source check: dose reduction ✅✅ (Eliquis label, SmPC); PAUSE schedule ✅ (WikiJournalClub); CHEST 2022 resume timing ✅. See Anticoagulation_Core sections 1 and 3.
Case 2 (Warfarin): INR 7.2, then a bleed
A 70 kg man on warfarin for AF has an INR of 7.2 and no bleeding. The resident orders vitamin K 10 mg IV. Two days later he has a GI bleed, INR 5.1.
Model answer: “Day 1: hold warfarin and recheck the INR. With INR 4.5 to 10 and no bleeding, vitamin K isn’t needed (Crowther, Ann Intern Med 2009), and 10 mg IV is too much: it risks warfarin resistance when we restart. Day 2, major bleed: vitamin K 10 mg IV slow infusion plus 4F-PCC. INR 4 to 6 is 35 units/kg, so 2,450 units, under the 3,500 max. Recheck INR 30 minutes after PCC per label.”
Source check: INR 4.5 to 10 ✅✅ (UMEM on Crowther; Sunnybrook); PCC dosing ✅✅ (4F_PCC); recheck timing ⚠️ [VERIFY label wording].
Case 3 (HIT): Day 7 on heparin, kidneys failing
A patient on a heparin drip for 7 days: platelets fell from 240 K to 95 K. New thrombosis in the left arm. CrCl 18. A heparin flush order is pending.
Model answer: “This looks like HIT: more than a 50% drop, 5 to 10 days in, plus a new clot. Reject the flush and stop all heparin, including flushes and enoxaparin. Send a PF4 antibody test. With CrCl 18, argatroban fits because it’s cleared by the liver; it raises the INR, which matters when we switch to warfarin. No warfarin until platelets recover, and no routine platelet transfusion. Add heparin to the allergy list.”
Source check: see Heparin HIT section ✅; warfarin start threshold ⚠️ [VERIFY ASH 2018].
Case 4 (Anticoag + L&D): Epidural on enoxaparin
A pregnant patient on enoxaparin 40 mg SC daily got her last dose at 0600. Anesthesia wants to place an epidural at 1400.
Model answer: “Too early. Prophylactic enoxaparin needs 12 hours before neuraxial placement, so not before 1800. If she were on a treatment dose, 24 hours. After the catheter comes out, wait at least 4 hours for the next dose. I’d call anesthesia and the OB team now so they can plan.”
Source check: ✅✅ (Enoxaparin label; ASRA via NYSORA). See Enoxaparin and Anticoagulation_Core section 4.
Case 5 (ID): C. diff on IV vancomycin
C. diff positive. Order: vancomycin 125 mg IV q6h.
Model answer: “Wrong route. IV vancomycin doesn’t reach the colon. Per IDSA 2021, fidaxomicin 200 mg PO BID for 10 days is preferred; vancomycin 125 mg PO QID for 10 days is an alternative. Call the prescriber and change it.”
Source check: ✅✅ (AAFP summary of IDSA 2021; UIC Drug Information Group).
Case 6 (ID + psych): Linezolid and sertraline
A VRE bacteremia patient on linezolid has her home sertraline 100 mg resumed.
Model answer: “Flag serotonin syndrome. The FDA warns about linezolid with serotonergic drugs. I’d call the team: weigh holding sertraline (it has a long washout) or an alternative such as daptomycin if it fits the infection, and if they continue both, monitor for agitation, fever, tremor and clonus. Document.”
Source check: ✅ (FDA safety communication).
Case 7 (Interaction): Ciprofloxacin with binders
Ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO BID; the patient also takes calcium carbonate TID and sevelamer.
Model answer: “Chelation cuts ciprofloxacin absorption. Give ciprofloxacin at least 2 hours before or 6 hours after calcium and binders. Also check the renal dose and other QT drugs.”
Source check: ✅ (ciprofloxacin label on DailyMed).
Case 8 (Renal): Morphine on hemodialysis
Order: morphine 4 mg IV q2h PRN pain, patient on hemodialysis.
Model answer: “Morphine’s active metabolites build up in kidney failure and cause sedation and neurotoxicity. Recommend a low dose of hydromorphone or fentanyl, and monitor sedation and breathing.”
Source check: ⚠️ [VERIFY with a renal dosing reference].
Case 9 (Safety): Insulin for hyperkalemia
Order: “Insulin regular 10U IV x1” for K 6.8 with peaked T waves. No dextrose ordered. CrCl 12.
Model answer: “Three things. Calcium gluconate 1 g IV first to stabilize the heart. ‘U’ is an ISMP Do Not Use abbreviation (read as 0 or 4), so rewrite as ‘10 units.’ And insulin needs dextrose 25 g; with CrCl 12, consider 5 units to lower hypoglycemia risk, and check glucose hourly for several hours.”
Source check: Do Not Use list ✅ (ISMP); 5 unit option ⚠️ [VERIFY]. See Insulin_IV_DKA.
Case 10 (Oncology safety): Methotrexate daily, vincristine in a syringe
Two orders on one patient: methotrexate 7.5 mg PO daily for rheumatoid arthritis (home med), and vincristine 2 mg prepared in a 10 mL syringe while intrathecal methotrexate is also scheduled.
Model answer: “Both are classic fatal errors. RA methotrexate is weekly: confirm with the patient and outpatient pharmacy, then correct to once weekly on a named day. Vincristine goes in a minibag, never a syringe, labeled ‘For intravenous use only. Fatal if given by other routes,’ and stays apart from intrathecal doses.”
Source check: ✅✅ (ISMP vincristine labeling; WHO alert 115); weekly methotrexate ✅ (ISMP Targeted Best Practices).

Note: the raw interview prep DKA case uses a potassium cutoff of 3.3 for adults. The 2024 adult consensus uses 3.5; see Insulin_IV_DKA.
Last verified: 2026-10-17.

cases/cases_codes_stroke_trauma.title: Cases_Codes_Stroke_Trauma
cases/cases_codes_stroke_trauma.content:
Practice Cases: Codes, Stroke, Trauma
All cases are invented for teaching. 60 seconds each, out loud. Top 10% = answer + source and year + exact order + monitoring.

Case 1 (Code): Dialysis patient in PEA
A 64 year old on hemodialysis who missed two sessions is in PEA. Peaked T waves were seen before the arrest.
Model answer: “Suspect hyperkalemia. Calcium chloride 1 g IV now, then insulin regular 10 units IV with dextrose 25 g, and sodium bicarbonate 50 mEq if acidotic. Keep epinephrine 1 mg every 3 to 5 minutes going; in nonshockable rhythms AHA 2025 says give it as early as possible. After ROSC, recheck potassium and glucose and plan dialysis.”
Case 2 (Code): Wrong dose risk
A nurse asks for “adenosine 6 mg” for a patient with a heart transplant.
Model answer: “Heart transplant patients are very sensitive to adenosine because the heart is denervated. Start with 3 mg. Same for patients on dipyridamole or carbamazepine, or if it’s given through a central line.”
Case 3 (Stroke): Tenecteplase
A 78 kg patient, last known well 2 hours ago, NIHSS 9, BP 192/104, on no anticoagulants. The team chooses tenecteplase.
Model answer: “BP has to be below 185/110 first: labetalol 10 to 20 mg IV, or start nicardipine 5 mg/h. Tenecteplase stroke dose is 0.25 mg/kg, which is 19.5 mg here, max 25 mg, as a single IV bolus over 5 seconds, using our weight band chart. Not the cardiac dose. Then BP below 180/105 for 24 hours and no antithrombotics for 24 hours. AHA/ASA 2026 lists tenecteplase as equally preferred to alteplase.”
Case 4 (Stroke): ICH on apixaban
An 82 year old on apixaban (last dose 4 hours ago) has an intracerebral hemorrhage. SBP 196.
Model answer: “Reverse with 4F-PCC 50 units/kg per our protocol; andexanet was withdrawn from the US market in 2025. Lower SBP to a target of 140, staying within 130 to 150 and avoiding drops below 130 (AHA/ASA 2022), with a nicardipine or clevidipine drip. Hold apixaban.”
Case 5 (Stroke): SAH
A patient with aneurysmal SAH has an order for nimodipine 60 mg IV every 4 hours.
Model answer: “Nimodipine is oral or by feeding tube only, never IV; there’s an FDA boxed warning because injecting capsule contents has caused deaths. The order should be 60 mg by mouth or tube every 4 hours for 21 days (AHA/ASA 2023). If her BP drops, 30 mg every 2 hours.”
Case 6 (Trauma): TXA timing
A motorcycle crash patient arrives 4 hours after injury with ongoing bleeding. The resident orders TXA.
Model answer: “CRASH-2 found TXA works best given early and may cause harm when started more than 3 hours after injury. At 4 hours it isn’t recommended. Let’s focus on balanced transfusion with calcium replacement guided by ionized calcium. Did EMS already give TXA?”
Case 7 (Trauma): Open fracture
A 130 kg patient with a type III open tibia fracture, no allergies.
Model answer: “Antibiotics within the hour (EAST). Cefazolin 3 g IV, since he’s over 120 kg, plus gram negative coverage for a type III per our order set. Check tetanus: if his history is unknown, Tdap plus tetanus immune globulin 250 units IM.”
Case 8 (Trauma): RSI choice
A trauma patient with 40% burns 3 days ago needs reintubation. Succinylcholine is ordered.
Model answer: “Avoid succinylcholine. After 24 to 48 hours, burn patients can have severe hyperkalemia from succinylcholine. Rocuronium 1 to 1.2 mg/kg is the alternative, with sugammadex available for rescue.”

cases/cases_ld_nicu_picu.title: Cases_LD_NICU_PICU
cases/cases_ld_nicu_picu.content:
Practice Cases: L&D, NICU, PICU
All cases are invented for teaching. Answer out loud in under 60 seconds, then check the model answer. Score yourself: Weak / Solid / Top 10%.
Top 10% = right answer + the source and year + the exact recommendation + what to monitor.

Case 1 (L&D): Magnesium at 2 a.m.
A 31 year old at 36 weeks with preeclampsia with severe features is on magnesium sulfate 2 g/h. The nurse calls: urine output has been 15 mL/h for 2 hours, respiratory rate 11, patellar reflexes absent.
Model answer: “Stop the magnesium now. This looks like magnesium toxicity: loss of reflexes and a respiratory rate under 12, with low urine output so it’s accumulating. Give calcium gluconate 1 g IV over about 3 minutes, support her breathing, and send a STAT magnesium level and creatinine. Call the OB now. When she’s stable and the level is back, restart at a lower rate per protocol if she still needs seizure prophylaxis.”
Source: ACOG Practice Bulletin 222 (2020). Linked: LD_Obstetrics_Core.
Case 2 (L&D): Hemorrhage order
Postpartum hemorrhage after vaginal delivery. Oxytocin is running. The OB asks for methylergonovine. The patient’s history shows preeclampsia this pregnancy.
Model answer: “Methylergonovine is contraindicated with hypertension and preeclampsia. Carboprost 250 mcg IM is the next option if she doesn’t have asthma, or misoprostol. Tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 minutes is recommended if we’re within 3 hours of birth (WOMAN trial). Would you like carboprost and TXA?”
Case 3 (L&D): GBS and an allergy
GBS positive patient in labor. Allergy: penicillin, “rash as a child.” Order: vancomycin.
Model answer: “A childhood rash without hives, anaphylaxis or a severe skin reaction is a low risk allergy. ACOG Committee Opinion 797 (2020) recommends cefazolin 2 g IV, then 1 g every 8 hours, for low risk penicillin allergy. Cefazolin counts as adequate prophylaxis for the baby; vancomycin doesn’t, and it adds nephrotoxicity risk. Can I change it to cefazolin?”
Case 4 (NICU): Decimal check
A 1.2 kg preterm infant. Order: gentamicin 12 mg IV every 24 hours.
Model answer: “That’s 10 mg/kg, about double the usual neonatal dose (around 4 to 5 mg/kg per dose depending on gestational age). It looks like a calculation error; at 4 to 5 mg/kg the dose would be about 4.8 to 6 mg. Preterm infants also often need a longer interval than every 24 hours. I’d hold it and call the prescriber to confirm the dose and interval from our neonatal chart, plus a level plan.”
Case 5 (NICU): Ceftriaxone in a jaundiced newborn
A 4 day old with jaundice and suspected sepsis. Order: ceftriaxone IV, and calcium gluconate is running for hypocalcemia.
Model answer: “Two problems. Ceftriaxone displaces bilirubin and should be avoided in hyperbilirubinemic neonates, and in neonates it must never be given with IV calcium because of fatal precipitates (FDA warning). Recommend cefepime or ceftazidime with ampicillin per our neonatal sepsis protocol.”
Case 6 (PICU): Seizure
A 22 kg 6 year old has been seizing for 7 minutes. IV access is in. Lorazepam is ordered.
Model answer: “Lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg is 2.2 mg IV (max 4 mg). It can repeat once in 5 minutes. If she’s still seizing, second line is levetiracetam 60 mg/kg, which is 1,320 mg IV, or fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg, which is 440 mg PE. ESETT showed similar efficacy among levetiracetam, fosphenytoin and valproate.”
Case 7 (PICU): Code doses
A 15 kg child in asystole.
Model answer: “Epinephrine 0.15 mg IV, which is 1.5 mL of the 0.1 mg/mL, every 3 to 5 minutes. PALS 2025 says give it as early as possible in nonshockable rhythms. If the rhythm changes to VF: shock 2 J/kg, which is 30 J, then 4 J/kg, and amiodarone 75 mg (5 mg/kg).”
Case 8 (PICU): DKA
A 30 kg 10 year old in DKA. Order: insulin 3 units IV bolus, then 3 units/h. K is 3.0.
Model answer: “Two changes. ISPAD 2022 recommends no insulin bolus in children, because of cerebral edema risk. And with K at 3.0, ISPAD says to start potassium replacement before insulin; many protocols hold insulin until K is at least 3.3 [VERIFY St. Mary’s cutoff]. Then start 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/h, which is 1.5 to 3 units/h. Have mannitol or 3% saline available for cerebral edema.”

clinical/adult_critical_care.title: Adult_Critical_Care
clinical/adult_critical_care.content:
Adult Critical Care: Pharmacist Core (Module 9)
Pharmacist’s job overnight in the ICU: pressors and drips right, analgesia before sedation, electrolytes corrected at a safe speed, glucose in range without lows, and nothing given that keeps a patient on the ventilator longer than needed.
Key: ✅✅ two independent sources · ✅ one source · ⚠️ [VERIFY]
Related: Norepinephrine · Insulin_IV_DKA · Potassium_Chloride_IV · ID_Core (sepsis) · IV_Compatibility · Codes_Resuscitation

1. Shock and pressors (SSC 2021)

Norepinephrine first; add vasopressin instead of raising norepinephrine; then epinephrine; dobutamine for heart dysfunction ✅ [1] · Norepinephrine.
MAP goal 65 ✅ Norepinephrine.
Steroids when norepinephrine or epinephrine is 0.25 mcg/kg/min or more for at least 4 h ✅ [1]; dose ⚠️ [VERIFY].

2. Pain, sedation and delirium (PADIS 2018)













































TopicRecommendationCheckOrder of careAnalgesia first, then sedation✅ [2]TargetLight sedation for most patients (RASS or SAS)✅ [2]SedativePropofol or dexmedetomidine over benzodiazepines; no preference between the two ⚠️; deep sedation (paralysis) usually propofol✅ [2]Pain toolsCPOT or BPS when the patient can’t report pain✅ [2]Pain adjunctsAcetaminophen; low dose ketamine after abdominal surgery; gabapentin or pregabalin for neuropathic pain; no routine IV lidocaine or NSAIDs✅ [2]DeliriumScreen with CAM-ICU or ICDSC; don’t give drugs to prevent it; no routine antipsychotics; dexmedetomidine when agitation is blocking extubation✅ [2]SleepNo melatonin recommendation; don’t use propofol for sleep✅ [2]
Propofol infusion syndrome (PRIS): risk rises above 4 mg/kg/h (about 67 mcg/kg/min) and after 48 h, plus catecholamines or steroids. Signs: metabolic acidosis, bradycardia, rhabdomyolysis, high triglycerides, AKI. Stop propofol ✅ [3]. Monitor triglycerides and CK on longer infusions; count propofol’s lipid calories (about 1.1 kcal/mL) in nutrition ⚠️ [VERIFY label].
3. Hyperkalemia






























StepDrug and doseCheckProtect the heartCalcium gluconate 1 g (10 mL of 10%) IV over 2 to 5 min; repeat in 5 min if ECG changes persist✅✅ [4][5]ShiftRegular insulin 10 units IV with dextrose 25 g (50 mL D50); 5 units if high hypoglycemia risk (kidney failure, low weight, elderly); check glucose hourly for 4 to 6 h✅✅ [4][5]Shift (adjunct)Nebulized albuterol 10 to 20 mg; sodium bicarbonate only if acidotic✅ [4]RemoveSodium zirconium cyclosilicate 10 g or patiromer 8.4 g; loop diuretic if kidneys work; dialysis✅✅ [4][5]
KDIGO severity: severe = K above 6.5, or 6.1 to 6.5 with ECG changes ✅ [5].
4. Hyponatremia

Severe symptoms (seizure, coma): 3% saline bolus 150 mL over 20 min, repeat if needed; aim for about a 5 mmol/L rise in the first hour ✅ [6]. US practice uses 100 mL boluses ⚠️ [VERIFY].
Limits: 10 mmol/L in the first 24 h, then 8 per 24 h (European) ✅✅ [6][7]. High risk (alcohol use disorder, low potassium, malnutrition, liver disease): 8 per 24 h max ✅ [7].
Overcorrection: stop hypertonic fluid; hypotonic fluid with or without desmopressin ✅ [6].
Debate: newer data (MacMillan 2023) suggest osmotic demyelination is rare and slow correction has its own risks; follow St. Mary’s protocol ✅ [7].

5. ICU glucose

Start an insulin infusion above 180 mg/dL; target 140 to 180 mg/dL (ADA, AACE) ✅✅ [8][9].
NICE-SUGAR: tight control (81 to 108) raised 90 day death (27.5% vs 24.9%) and severe lows (6.8% vs 0.5%) ✅ [9].
DKA is its own protocol: Insulin_IV_DKA.

6. Other daily ICU checks

Stress ulcer prophylaxis only with a real risk factor (ventilation over 48 h, coagulopathy); stop at transfer ⚠️ [VERIFY guideline].
VTE prophylaxis unless bleeding; trauma uses enoxaparin per Trauma_Core.
Drips through compatible lines (IV_Compatibility); concentrated drips central.
Renal dosing as CrCl changes; augmented clearance in young trauma patients ⚠️ [VERIFY].

Sources

UIC Drug Information Group: SSC 2021 updates

clinical/anticoagulation_core.title: Anticoagulation_Core
clinical/anticoagulation_core.content:
Anticoagulation: Pharmacist Core (Module 7)
Pharmacist’s job: right drug, right dose for kidney function and weight, right monitoring, no duplicate anticoagulants, safe timing around procedures and epidurals, and fast reversal.
Key: ✅✅ two independent sources · ✅ one source · ⚠️ [VERIFY]
Drug pages: Heparin · Enoxaparin · 4F_PCC. Reversal table: Stroke_Core section 3.

1. DOAC dosing (the numbers you verify every shift)













































DrugAtrial fibrillationVTE treatmentKidney and other adjustmentsCheckSourcesApixaban5 mg BID10 mg BID x 7 days, then 5 mg BID; after 6 months, 2.5 mg BID for preventionAF: 2.5 mg BID if 2 of 3: age 80 or older, weight 60 kg or less, SCr 1.5 or higher✅✅[1] SmPC; [9] Pfizer label (India). Dialysis: NVAF trials excluded dialysis; VTE needs no renal adjustment per [9] ⚠️ [VERIFY US label wording]Rivaroxaban20 mg daily with the evening meal; 15 mg if CrCl 15 to 5015 mg BID with food x 21 days, then 20 mg daily with food15 and 20 mg tablets must be taken with food✅✅[2] EBM Consult monograph (US label); [3] GlobalRPh renal page (avoid if CrCl below 15 in AF, below 30 in VTE)Dabigatran150 mg BID; 75 mg BID if CrCl 15 to 30After 5 to 10 days of parenteral therapy, 150 mg BID ⚠️Swallow capsules whole (opening raises exposure); P-gp interactions with renal impairment✅ (AF)[4] FDA label (2012 version)Edoxaban60 mg daily; 30 mg if CrCl 15 to 50; don’t use in AF if CrCl above 95 (less effective)After 5 to 10 days parenteral; 60 mg daily (30 mg if CrCl 15 to 50, weight 60 kg or less, or certain P-gp inhibitors)With or without food; tablets may be crushed✅[13] Drugs.com label summary; [14] label PDF (HemOnc) to recheck
Classic catches: rivaroxaban 15 or 20 mg without food; apixaban reduced to 2.5 mg with only one criterion; DOAC plus a heparin product at the same time; DOAC in a prosthetic or mechanical heart valve (not recommended per label) ✅ [9]; strong CYP3A4 and P-gp inducers or inhibitors.
2. Warfarin

Supratherapeutic INR, no bleeding: INR 4.5 to 10: hold doses; oral vitamin K is usually not needed (Crowther, Ann Intern Med 2009: vitamin K 1.25 mg did not reduce bleeding vs placebo) ✅✅ [5][6]. INR above 10: hold and give oral vitamin K 2.5 to 5 mg ✅ [6].
Major bleeding: hold warfarin, vitamin K 10 mg IV, plus 4F-PCC by INR ✅✅ [6]4F_PCC.
Route: oral for non urgent reversal; IV when faster reversal is needed; avoid IM; avoid high doses (5 to 10 mg) without bleeding because they cause warfarin resistance ✅ [6].
Interactions to catch: antibiotics (TMP SMX, fluoroquinolones, metronidazole, fluconazole), amiodarone, rifampin; new diet or illness.

3. Around procedures (CHEST 2022 and PAUSE)

Warfarin: stop about 5 days before ✅✅ [7] (BRIDGE protocol); [8] UConn handout.
Bridging: CHEST 2022 recommends against bridging in AF (strong) and suggests against it for mechanical valves or VTE (conditional) ✅ [10]. BRIDGE trial: no bridging was noninferior for clots and caused less major bleeding (1.3% vs 3.2%) ✅ [7]. Very high risk patients (for example a mechanical mitral valve or a clot in the last 3 months) are often still bridged per cardiology or hematology ✅ [8] ⚠️ [VERIFY St. Mary’s policy].
DOACs: stop 1 to 2 days before (dabigatran 1 to 4 days, longer if CrCl below 50); resume about 24 h after low or moderate bleed risk procedures, 48 to 72 h after high bleed risk ✅✅ [10][11] PAUSE. No bridging for DOACs ✅✅ [8][11].
PAUSE schedule (apixaban, rivaroxaban; dabigatran with CrCl 50 or higher): low bleed risk: skip the day before and the day of surgery; high bleed risk: skip 2 days before and the day of ✅ [11].
Aspirin: generally continue for elective noncardiac surgery ✅ [10].

4. Epidural and spinal timing (ASRA)















































DrugStop before neuraxialRestart after catheter removalCheckSourcesEnoxaparin prophylaxis12 h4 h (label)✅✅EnoxaparinEnoxaparin treatment dose24 h✅✅EnoxaparinApixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban72 h6 h✅[12] NYSORA summary of ASRA 2021Dabigatran120 h by default (shorter by CrCl)6 h✅[12]WarfarinNormal INR (usually about 5 days off)⚠️[VERIFY ASRA current edition]
5. Pharmacist verification checklist

Indication and the right dose for it.
CrCl (Cockcroft Gault, actual weight unless protocol says otherwise), weight, age, platelets, hemoglobin.
Only one anticoagulant active (check heparin flushes and SC prophylaxis too).
Interactions (CYP3A4 and P-gp; warfarin antibiotics).
Procedure or epidural coming? Hold times.
Reversal plan known for this drug.

clinical/codes_resuscitation.title: Codes_Resuscitation
clinical/codes_resuscitation.content:
Codes and Resuscitation: Pharmacist Core
Pharmacist’s job at a code: know the crash cart, prepare and hand off the right dose, call out timing (epinephrine every 3 to 5 minutes), suggest reversible causes and their drugs, set up post arrest drips, and document.
Sources: AHA Guidelines for CPR and ECC (2025; adult ALS, PALS Part 8, NRP Part 5); AHA 2023 focused update on adult ACLS (toxicology and drug use); ASRA local anesthetic systemic toxicity checklist; MHAUS (malignant hyperthermia). Pediatric doses: PICU_Core. Neonatal doses: NICU_Core.

1. Adult cardiac arrest drugs (AHA 2025: no major drug changes)



































DrugDoseWhenEpinephrine1 mg IV/IO every 3 to 5 minutesNonshockable: as soon as possible. Shockable: after initial defibrillation attempts failAmiodarone300 mg IV/IO push, then 150 mgRefractory VF or pulseless VTLidocaine1 to 1.5 mg/kg, then 0.5 to 0.75 mg/kgAlternative to amiodaroneVasopressinNot in the 2025 algorithmEpinephrine is the only vasopressor in the arrest algorithmCalcium, bicarbonate, magnesiumNot routineOnly for specific causes (below)
IV is preferred for drug delivery; IO if IV can’t be placed quickly (AHA 2025).
2. Reversible causes and the drug you hand them (H’s and T’s)









































CauseDrugHyperkalemiaCalcium chloride 1 g IV (or calcium gluconate 3 g), insulin regular 10 units IV + dextrose 25 g, sodium bicarbonate 50 mEq if acidoticHypoglycemiaDextrose 50% 25 g (50 mL)Torsades / hypomagnesemiaMagnesium sulfate 1 to 2 g IV push in arrestOpioid overdoseNaloxone 0.4 to 2 mg IV, or 4 mg intranasal; ventilation comes first in arrestTricyclic overdose (wide QRS)Sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mEq/kgLocal anesthetic toxicityLipid emulsion 20%: 1.5 mL/kg bolus over 2 to 3 minutes, then 0.25 mL/kg/min (ASRA). Use smaller epinephrine doses (1 mcg/kg or less)Pulmonary embolismAlteplase 50 mg IV bolus can be considered in suspected PE arrest [VERIFY institutional protocol]Beta blocker or calcium channel blocker overdoseHigh dose insulin, calcium, glucagon (beta blocker), vasopressors
3. Peri arrest

Bradycardia: atropine 1 mg IV every 3 to 5 minutes (max 3 mg); if no response, epinephrine infusion 2 to 10 mcg/min or dopamine 5 to 20 mcg/kg/min, or pacing.
Stable SVT: adenosine 6 mg rapid push, then 12 mg (use 3 mg if central line, heart transplant, or patient on dipyridamole or carbamazepine; caffeine and theophylline reduce effect).
Anaphylaxis: epinephrine 0.5 mg IM (1 mg/mL) in the thigh, repeat every 5 to 15 minutes; refractory: epinephrine infusion.
Malignant hyperthermia (after succinylcholine or volatile anesthetic): dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg IV, repeat to effect (MHAUS). Know where the MH cart is and which product (Ryanodex reconstitutes much faster than Dantrium).

4. After ROSC (post cardiac arrest care)

Avoid hypotension: common targets SBP at least 90 and MAP at least 65 mmHg; norepinephrine is the usual first vasopressor.
Temperature control and fever prevention in comatose patients [VERIFY 2025 duration and target wording].
Avoid hypoxia and hyperoxia (SpO2 about 92 to 98%).
Check glucose, potassium, magnesium; sedation and analgesia after intubation.

5. Your code checklist (pharmacist)

Bring or open the code tray; confirm the patient’s weight and allergies.
Track epinephrine timing out loud (“Epi due in one minute”).
Pre draw amiodarone 300 mg and the next epinephrine.
Ask “Any chance of hyperkalemia, overdose or PE?” and have the drug ready.
Mix post ROSC drips in standard concentrations (norepinephrine, amiodarone infusion, sedation).
Document drugs given and times; replace the tray per policy.

Verify locally at St. Mary’s

Pharmacist role on the code team for adult and pediatric codes, days vs nights.
Crash cart contents and who restocks.
Post arrest order set and temperature control protocol.
Where lipid emulsion, dantrolene and digoxin immune fab are stocked.

clinical/id_core.title: ID_Core
clinical/id_core.content:
Infectious Diseases and Stewardship: Pharmacist Core (Module 8)
Pharmacist’s job: get the first dose out fast, pick the right drug for the syndrome and the patient’s history, dose for weight and kidneys, sort out allergy labels, then narrow, switch to oral and stop on time.
Key: ✅✅ two independent sources · ✅ one source · ⚠️ [VERIFY]
Regimens by infection: Antimicrobial_Guide. Drug pages: Vancomycin · Gentamicin. Pediatric and neonatal: NICU_Core · PICU_Core.

1. Sepsis (Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)























































PointRecommendationCheckTiming, shock or sepsis likelyAntimicrobials within 1 hour (strong)✅ [1]Timing, possible sepsis without shockWithin 3 hours after rapid assessment (weak)✅ [1]MRSA coverageOnly if high MRSA risk✅ [1]Two gram negative agentsOnly if high risk for multidrug resistance; stop the second once susceptibilities return✅ [1]Beta lactam maintenanceProlonged infusion suggested over standard infusion✅ [1]FluidsAt least 30 mL/kg crystalloid in the first 3 h; balanced crystalloids suggested over saline✅ [1]PressorsNorepinephrine first; add vasopressin rather than raising norepinephrine✅ [1] · NorepinephrineSteroidsSuggested when norepinephrine or epinephrine is 0.25 mcg/kg/min or more for at least 4 h✅ [1]; dose (hydrocortisone 200 mg/day) ⚠️ [VERIFY]StoppingReassess daily; procalcitonin plus clinical judgment can guide stopping✅ [1]
Pharmacist moves: first doses go STAT; give a full loading dose even when kidney function is poor, then adjust maintenance; vancomycin load 20 to 35 mg/kg (Vancomycin).
2. Beta lactam allergy

Cross reactivity between penicillins and cephalosporins comes from the R1 side chain, not the beta lactam ring ✅ [2].
Cefazolin shares no side chains with other US beta lactams, so cross reactivity is near zero ✅ [2].
2022 drug allergy practice parameter: with an unconfirmed, non anaphylactic penicillin history, any cephalosporin can be given without testing ✅ [2].
Severe delayed reactions (SJS, TEN, DRESS) mean avoid the class and call allergy or ID ⚠️ [VERIFY parameter wording].
Ask: what happened, when, how was it treated, and has the patient taken a beta lactam since? Clarifying a label is one of the highest value pharmacist interventions.

3. C. difficile (IDSA 2021)
Fidaxomicin 200 mg PO BID x 10 days preferred; vancomycin 125 mg PO QID x 10 days alternative. IV vancomycin does not treat C. diff ✅✅ [3][4]. See Cases_Anticoag_and_Verification case 5.
4. IV to PO switch
Stable, afebrile, improving, working gut, taking other oral meds. Good oral options: fluoroquinolones, linezolid, metronidazole, TMP SMX, doxycycline, fluconazole. Separate fluoroquinolones and tetracyclines from calcium, iron, magnesium and binders ✅ (labels). Not for meningitis, endocarditis or S. aureus bacteremia without ID input ⚠️ [VERIFY]. cUTI with gram negative bacteremia can step down to oral when improving ✅ [5].
5. Daily catches

Duplicate anaerobic coverage: metronidazole plus piperacillin tazobactam or a carbapenem ⚠️ [VERIFY local policy].
Cefepime and kidneys: accumulation can cause neurotoxicity; dose by CrCl ⚠️ [VERIFY label].
Vancomycin plus piperacillin tazobactam: more AKI; watch SCr (Vancomycin).
Linezolid: serotonin syndrome with SSRIs and SNRIs; low platelets with long courses ✅ (FDA).
Ceftriaxone plus IV calcium in neonates: contraindicated (NICU_Core).
Asymptomatic bacteriuria: don’t treat positive urine cultures without symptoms (except pregnancy and before urologic procedures) ✅ [6] ⚠️ [VERIFY exceptions].
Durations are shorter than habit: CAP at least 5 days, HAP 7 days [10], cUTI 7 days (5 to 7 with a fluoroquinolone), cellulitis about 5 days ✅✅ [7][5][8].

6. Stewardship workflow (every antibiotic, day 2 to 3)

Cultures back? Narrow.
MRSA nares negative? Consider stopping vancomycin for pneumonia (negative predictive value above 95%) ✅ [9].
Oral option? Switch.
Stop date written?

Sources

clinical/iv_room_core.title: IV_Room_Core
clinical/iv_room_core.content:
IV Room and Sterile Compounding: Pharmacist Core (Module 10)
Pharmacist’s job: nothing leaves the IV room unless the product matches the order, the concentration fits the line, the label is right, and the beyond use date (BUD) fits the USP 797 category.
Key: ✅✅ two independent sources · ✅ one source · ⚠️ [VERIFY] · Drug rules: IV_Compatibility

1. USP 797 (2023) categories and BUDs





















































CategoryWhere madeBUD room tempBUD refrigeratedFrozenCheckCategory 1ISO 5 hood in an unclassified segregated compounding area12 h24 h✅✅ [1][2]Category 2, aseptic from sterile ingredients, no sterility testISO 5 hood in a classified cleanroom suite4 days10 days45 days✅✅ [1][2]Category 2, terminally sterilized with sterility testingCleanroom45 days60 days90 days✅✅ [1][2]Category 3Cleanroom plus extra testing and monitoringUp to 90 daysUp to 120 daysUp to 180 days✅ [1]Immediate useEmergencies; start within 4 h of prep⚠️ [VERIFY USP chapter]
BUD can never be longer than the drug’s own stability allows ✅ [1].
2. Rooms and garbing

ISO 5 = hood (primary engineering control); ISO 7 = buffer room; ISO 8 = ante room ⚠️ [VERIFY USP].
First air: never block HEPA air between the filter and the critical site.
Garb dirty to clean: shoe covers, hair cover, mask, wash hands, gown, sanitize, sterile gloves ⚠️ [VERIFY St. Mary’s SOP].
Hazardous drugs (USP 800): negative pressure room, biological safety cabinet or isolator, two pairs of chemo gloves, closed system transfer devices ⚠️ [VERIFY].

3. The product check (every bag, every syringe)

Patient, drug, dose, diluent, volume, final concentration against the order.
Vials and syringes used match the dose (pull back check).
Concentration fits the line: peripheral or central (IV_Compatibility).
Rate math on the label (units/h ÷ units/mL = mL/h).
Container, tubing, filter and light protection.
BUD matches the USP 797 category and drug stability.
Look at the bag: particles, cloudiness, leaks.
Peds and neonatal: recheck weight based math and the max dose; watch preservatives.

4. Classic IV room catches

Phenytoin in dextrose, or pushed faster than 50 mg/min.
Liposomal amphotericin in saline.
Nitroglycerin in a PVC bag.
Amiodarone above 2 mg/mL going peripheral.
PN above 900 mOsm/L going peripheral.
0.22 micron filter on a lipid containing PN.
Vincristine in a syringe.
10 fold rate errors (144 vs 14.4 mL/h).
A Category 1 product labeled with a 48 h refrigerated BUD.

Practice these in the simulator (My Tools, IV room cases).
Sources

Wolters Kluwer: USP 797 categories and BUDs
Helmer: USP 797 cold storage and BUD table

clinical/ld_obstetrics_core.title: LD_Obstetrics_Core
clinical/ld_obstetrics_core.content:
Labor & Delivery: Pharmacist Core
Pharmacist’s job on L&D: verify high alert infusions (magnesium, oxytocin), get emergency drugs out fast (hypertension, hemorrhage, eclampsia), check every drug for pregnancy and lactation safety, and catch the classic contraindications.
Sources: ACOG Practice Bulletin 222 (2020, gestational hypertension and preeclampsia); ACOG Committee Opinion 767 (2019, acute severe hypertension); ACOG Committee Opinion 797 (2020, GBS prophylaxis); ACOG Practice Bulletin 183 (2017, postpartum hemorrhage); WOMAN trial (Lancet 2017, TXA); ISMP High Alert list (magnesium sulfate IV, oxytocin IV).

1. Acute severe hypertension (preeclampsia, eclampsia)
Threshold: SBP 160 or higher, or DBP 110 or higher, persistent for 15 minutes. Treat within 30 to 60 minutes (ACOG CO 767, 2019).

























DrugRegimen (ACOG CO 767)Pharmacist watchLabetalol IV20 mg over 2 min; repeat BP in 10 min; if high, 40 mg; then 80 mg; if still high, switch to hydralazine. Max 300 mg cumulativeAvoid in asthma, heart failure, heart block; bradycardia (maternal and neonatal)Hydralazine IV5 to 10 mg over 2 min; repeat BP in 20 min; if high, 10 mg; if still high, switch to labetalolMaternal hypotension and tachycardia; watch fetal heart rateNifedipine immediate release PO10 mg; repeat BP in 20 min; if high, 20 mg; then 20 mg; if still high, switch to labetalolOral only. Never sublingual. Good option with no IV access
Quote it: “ACOG recommends treating BP of 160 or 110 within 30 to 60 minutes with IV labetalol, IV hydralazine or immediate release oral nifedipine.”
2. Magnesium sulfate (ISMP high alert)
Uses: seizure prophylaxis in preeclampsia with severe features; eclampsia treatment; fetal neuroprotection before 32 weeks.

Dose (ACOG PB 222): 4 to 6 g IV load over 15 to 20 minutes (FDA label: over 15 minutes), then 1 to 2 g/h. Continue 24 hours after delivery (or after the last seizure). IM option: 10 g (5 g each buttock), then 5 g IM every 4 hours.
Recurrent seizure on magnesium: additional 2 to 4 g IV over 5 minutes.
Renal: magnesium is renally cleared. FDA label for severe renal impairment or oliguria: 4 g load, then 1 g/h, max 20 g per 48 h, with serum levels; keep urine output at least 100 mL per 4 hours. See Magnesium_Sulfate.
Monitoring: deep tendon reflexes, respiratory rate (concern if under 12), urine output, mental status, oxygen saturation; serum magnesium if renal impairment or toxicity is suspected.
Toxicity (FDA label): reflexes weaken above about 4 mEq/L; respiratory paralysis risk at about 10 mEq/L. Label eclampsia target 2.5 to 5 mEq/L (3 to 6 mg/dL). Textbooks quote higher thresholds; follow the label and St. Mary’s protocol. Corrected 2026-10-17 (earlier version used higher textbook numbers).
Antidote: stop the infusion; calcium gluconate 1 g IV (10 mL of 10%) over about 3 minutes; support ventilation.
Safety: use premixed bags and a dedicated pump channel; the classic error is the loading bag running at the maintenance setting or a 20 g bag running wide open (ISMP). Avoid with myasthenia gravis.

Quote it: “Loss of deep tendon reflexes comes before respiratory depression; that’s why nurses check reflexes on magnesium, and the antidote is 1 g of calcium gluconate.”
3. Oxytocin (ISMP high alert)

Standardized concentration and pump library are the safety net [VERIFY St. Mary’s concentration, for example 30 units in 500 mL].
Watch for tachysystole (more than 5 contractions in 10 minutes) and water intoxication (hyponatremia) with long, high dose infusions.
Look alike risk: oxytocin bags near magnesium bags. Check the label every time.

4. Postpartum hemorrhage (ACOG PB 183, 2017; WOMAN 2017)
Order of use and the one contraindication to remember for each:



































DrugTypical doseDo not use ifOxytocin10 to 40 units in 500 to 1,000 mL IV infusion, or 10 units IM(first line)Methylergonovine0.2 mg IM every 2 to 4 hoursHypertension or preeclampsiaCarboprost (15 methyl PGF2 alpha)250 mcg IM every 15 to 90 minutes, max 8 doses (2 mg)AsthmaMisoprostol600 to 1,000 mcg rectal, sublingual or oral, once(fever and shivering are common)Tranexamic acid1 g IV over 10 minutes; may repeat 1 g after 30 minutes if bleeding continuesGive within 3 hours of birth (WOMAN trial)
Quote it: “No methylergonovine in hypertension, no carboprost in asthma, and TXA within 3 hours.”
5. GBS prophylaxis in labor (ACOG CO 797, 2020)





























SituationRegimenNo penicillin allergyPenicillin G 5 million units IV, then 2.5 to 3 million units IV every 4 hours until deliveryAlternativeAmpicillin 2 g IV, then 1 g IV every 4 hoursPenicillin allergy, low risk for anaphylaxisCefazolin 2 g IV, then 1 g IV every 8 hoursHigh risk allergy, isolate clindamycin susceptibleClindamycin 900 mg IV every 8 hoursHigh risk allergy, resistant or unknownVancomycin 20 mg/kg IV every 8 hours (max 2 g per dose)
Adequate prophylaxis = a beta lactam (penicillin, ampicillin or cefazolin) started at least 4 hours before delivery. This matters to the NICU team, so it is worth documenting clearly.
Many “penicillin allergies” are low risk; allergy clarification is a high value pharmacist intervention here.
6. Other L&D drugs to know

Antenatal corticosteroids: betamethasone 12 mg IM every 24 hours for 2 doses (24 0/7 to 33 6/7 weeks; late preterm use has specific criteria) (ACOG CO 713, 2017; updated guidance [VERIFY]).
Tocolytics: nifedipine; indomethacin only before 32 weeks and for no more than 48 hours (ductus arteriosus constriction, oligohydramnios). Terbutaline: FDA boxed warning against prolonged use (beyond 48 to 72 hours) for preterm labor.
Rh(D) immune globulin: 300 mcg IM at about 28 weeks and within 72 hours after delivery when an Rh negative mother has an Rh positive infant.
Epidural and neuraxial: know your anticoagulation timing rules before neuraxial procedures (ASRA guidelines) [module 7].
Lactation: use LactMed (NIH) as the free reference.

Verify locally at St. Mary’s

Magnesium order set: load, maintenance, renal adjustment, level timing.
Hypertension in pregnancy order set and which agent is first line.
Oxytocin concentration and pump library.
PPH kit or cart contents and who brings it.
GBS order set and allergy pathway.

clinical/nicu_core.title: NICU_Core
clinical/nicu_core.content:
NICU: Pharmacist Core
Pharmacist’s job in the NICU: make sure the dose is right for this baby’s weight and age, the concentration and volume are safe, the excipients are safe, and the interval fits the baby’s kidneys. Neonatal doses are tiny, so a decimal error is a 10 fold overdose.
Sources: AHA/AAP Neonatal Resuscitation Guidelines (2025); NRP Textbook 8th ed.; AAP Red Book (current edition); AAP Clinical Practice Guideline on hyperbilirubinemia (2022); ASHP/IDSA/PIDS/SIDP vancomycin consensus guideline (2020, includes pediatrics); ISMP pediatric safety guidance. Dosing references: Neofax or Lexicomp Pediatric and Neonatal (use what St. Mary’s uses).

1. The vocabulary you must use correctly

GA (gestational age): weeks in utero at birth.
PNA (postnatal age): days since birth.
PMA (postmenstrual age): GA + PNA in weeks. Many neonatal dosing intervals are based on PMA and PNA.
Birth weight vs dosing weight: know which one the order uses. Babies often drop weight the first week.
Term: 37 weeks or more. Preterm: under 37. Extremely preterm: under 28.

2. Safety rules that prevent the famous errors

Weight in kg, every time. Check the weight is current and plausible for age.
Check mg/kg/dose vs mg/kg/day. This is the most common pediatric error type.
10 fold errors: trailing zeros (never “1.0 mg”), leading zeros (always “0.1 mg”). Double check any dose that is a round number for a tiny baby.
Heparin: neonatal line flushes and infusions use very low concentrations. Wrong strength heparin vials have caused infant deaths (ISMP has documented cases). Verify the concentration on every heparin order.
Excipients: benzyl alcohol (gasping syndrome), propylene glycol, polysorbate, ethanol. Choose preservative free products for neonates.
Volume: a 600 g baby cannot take adult flush volumes. Count flush and dilution volume in the fluid total.
Independent double check for high alert drugs and all neonatal TPN.

3. Delivery room and resuscitation (AHA/AAP 2025; NRP)

Ventilation is the priority. 2025 update: ventilation rate 30 to 60 per minute; deferred cord clamping for 60 seconds or longer in vigorous infants.
Epinephrine: use 0.1 mg/mL (1 mg/10 mL). IV or UVC: 0.02 mg/kg (range 0.01 to 0.03 mg/kg) every 3 to 5 minutes. Endotracheal: 0.1 mg/kg (range 0.05 to 0.1). The IV route is preferred (NRP 8th ed.) [VERIFY against 2025 Part 5 text].
Volume expansion: normal saline 10 mL/kg over 5 to 10 minutes for suspected hypovolemia.
Pharmacist role: have the neonatal code doses calculated by weight before delivery for high risk births, if St. Mary’s uses a pre calculated sheet.

4. Routine newborn medications

Vitamin K (phytonadione): 0.5 to 1 mg IM once, to prevent vitamin K deficiency bleeding (AAP). Parents who refuse: document and educate.
Erythromycin 0.5% ophthalmic ointment: once, both eyes, for gonococcal ophthalmia prophylaxis.
Hepatitis B vaccine: within 24 hours; plus HBIG within 12 hours if the mother is HBsAg positive.

5. Neonatal sepsis (AAP Red Book; AAP clinical reports 2018 and 2019)

Early onset (first 72 hours): ampicillin + gentamicin.
Late onset: usually vancomycin (or nafcillin or oxacillin) + gentamicin, or a cephalosporin per unit protocol.
Meningitis concern: ampicillin + a third or fourth generation cephalosporin such as cefepime or ceftazidime (cefotaxime is no longer available in the US) [VERIFY St. Mary’s choice].
Ceftriaxone: avoid in neonates with hyperbilirubinemia (displaces bilirubin), and never give with IV calcium containing solutions in neonates (fatal precipitates; FDA).
HSV: acyclovir 20 mg/kg IV every 8 hours (adjust for kidney function); watch for nephrotoxicity and neutropenia.

6. Gentamicin and vancomycin in neonates

Gentamicin: extended interval dosing; dose and interval depend on GA or PMA and PNA. Example only: a term neonate is often 4 mg/kg every 24 hours; preterm babies get longer intervals (every 36 to 48 hours). Use the unit’s chart (Neofax or Lexicomp). Draw levels per protocol.
Vancomycin: the 2020 consensus guideline recommends AUC guided dosing in pediatrics and neonates where possible; know whether St. Mary’s uses AUC (Bayesian software) or troughs for neonates.

7. Other NICU drugs you will see








































DrugUseKey pointsCaffeine citrateApnea of prematurityLoad 20 mg/kg, then 5 to 10 mg/kg once daily. Caffeine citrate 2 mg = caffeine base 1 mg; know which salt the order usesSurfactant (poractant, beractant, calfactant)Respiratory distress syndromeGiven intratracheally; dose by product, mL/kg differs per productIndomethacin, ibuprofen lysine, acetaminophen IVPDA closureWatch urine output, platelets, GI bleeding (NSAIDs)Morphine, methadoneNeonatal opioid withdrawal syndromeMany units now use Eat, Sleep, Console first, which lowers medication usePhenobarbital, levetiracetamNeonatal seizuresPhenobarbital is still a common first line in neonates [VERIFY unit protocol]DextroseHypoglycemiaD10W 2 mL/kg IV bolus (200 mg/kg), then infusion; avoid concentrated dextrose peripherally
8. Neonatal TPN (with Module 10)

Calcium and phosphate solubility is the biggest compounding risk; neonates need high amounts of both. Use the solubility curve and add phosphate first, calcium last.
Cysteine improves calcium and phosphate solubility and is commonly added for neonates.
Lipid dose limits and monitoring triglycerides; know whether the unit uses SMOFlipid or Intralipid.
Every neonatal TPN gets an independent double check.

9. Hyperbilirubinemia (AAP CPG 2022)
Pharmacist angle: drugs that displace bilirubin (ceftriaxone, sulfonamides) are avoided in jaundiced neonates.
Verify locally at St. Mary’s

Neonatal dosing reference used (Neofax or Lexicomp) and the gentamicin interval chart.
Standard concentrations for neonatal drips (dopamine, epinephrine, morphine, fentanyl, insulin, heparin).
NICU level (St. Mary’s lists a Level III NICU) and who verifies orders on nights.
Empiric sepsis and meningitis regimens.
Pre calculated neonatal code sheet: who makes it.

clinical/picu_core.title: PICU_Core
clinical/picu_core.content:
PICU and Pediatric Emergencies: Pharmacist Core
Pharmacist’s job in the PICU: weight based emergency doses without errors, safe standard concentration drips, sedation and withdrawal plans, and adult max doses as the ceiling.
Sources: AHA/AAP Pediatric Advanced Life Support guideline (2025, Part 8, Circulation 2025;152 suppl 2); Neurocritical Care Society and American Epilepsy Society status epilepticus guidelines (AES 2016; ESETT trial, NEJM 2019); ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines, DKA (2022); AAP Clinical Practice Guideline on maintenance IV fluids (2018); SCCM PANDEM guidelines for pediatric ICU pain, agitation, neuromuscular blockade, delirium and iatrogenic withdrawal (Pediatr Crit Care Med, 2022).

1. The pediatric rules

Dose in mg/kg, but never exceed the adult dose. A 70 kg teenager gets an adult dose.
Use the measured weight in kg. For obese children, know whether the drug uses actual or ideal weight.
Standard concentrations matched to the smart pump library; no custom concentrations unless required.
Check the volume can actually be measured (very small volumes need dilution).

2. PALS code doses (AHA 2025)




























































DrugDoseNotesEpinephrine (0.1 mg/mL)0.01 mg/kg IV/IO (0.1 mL/kg), max 1 mg, every 3 to 5 minutes. ETT: 0.1 mg/kg2025: give as early as possible in nonshockable rhythmsAmiodarone5 mg/kg IV/IO bolus (max 300 mg), may repeat up to 15 mg/kg totalFor shock refractory VF or pulseless VTLidocaine1 mg/kg IV/IOAlternative to amiodaroneAdenosine0.1 mg/kg rapid push (max 6 mg); second dose 0.2 mg/kg (max 12 mg)SVT; rapid flush, closest portAtropine0.02 mg/kg IV (max single dose 0.5 mg)Bradycardia from vagal tone or AV blockCalcium chloride 10%20 mg/kg (0.2 mL/kg) IV/IO, central preferredHyperkalemia, hypocalcemia, calcium channel blocker overdoseCalcium gluconate 10%60 mg/kg (0.6 mL/kg) IVPeripheral friendly option [VERIFY dose in St. Mary’s sheet]Dextrose0.5 to 1 g/kg (D10W 5 to 10 mL/kg)HypoglycemiaSodium bicarbonate1 mEq/kgNot routine; hyperkalemia or tricyclic overdoseDefibrillation2 J/kg, then 4 J/kg, max 10 J/kg or adult doseNot a drug, but you’ll hear it
Quote it: “PALS 2025 emphasizes epinephrine as early as possible in nonshockable arrest; the dose is 0.01 mg/kg of the 0.1 mg/mL, max 1 mg.”
3. Status epilepticus






























TimeStepDose0 to 5 minStabilize, check glucoseDextrose if low5 to 20 minBenzodiazepineLorazepam 0.1 mg/kg IV (max 4 mg), may repeat once; or midazolam IM 0.2 mg/kg (max 10 mg); or diazepam rectal20 to 40 minSecond line (ESETT: similar efficacy)Levetiracetam 60 mg/kg IV (max 4,500 mg); or fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg (max 1,500 mg PE); or valproate 40 mg/kg (max 3,000 mg)40+ minRefractoryInfusion (midazolam, pentobarbital, ketamine) with ICU and EEG
Pharmacist watch: fosphenytoin is dosed in PE (phenytoin equivalents); valproate is avoided in suspected mitochondrial or metabolic disease and in young children with unknown liver disease.
4. Pediatric DKA (ISPAD 2022)

Fluids first: 10 to 20 mL/kg isotonic bolus.
Insulin 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/h IV, no bolus, started after the first hour of fluids.
Potassium: if the child is hypokalemic, start potassium replacement before insulin (ISPAD 2022); many protocols hold insulin until K is at least 3.3 [VERIFY St. Mary’s cutoff]. If K is normal, add it with insulin; if high, wait for urine output. Adults are different: the 2024 adult consensus holds insulin until K is above 3.5 (see Insulin_IV_DKA).
Add dextrose when glucose falls to about 250 to 300 mg/dL (two bag system).
Cerebral edema (headache, falling heart rate, rising BP, change in mental status): mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg over 10 to 15 min, or 3% saline 2.5 to 5 mL/kg. Have it available.

5. Rapid sequence intubation (pediatric)





























DrugDoseKetamine1 to 2 mg/kg IVEtomidate0.3 mg/kg IV (adrenal suppression; avoid in septic shock per many protocols)Rocuronium1 to 1.2 mg/kg IVSuccinylcholine2 mg/kg in infants, 1 to 1.5 mg/kg in children (avoid in hyperkalemia, neuromuscular disease, burns or crush after 24 to 48 h)Atropine premedicationNot routine; consider for infants or if bradycardia is likely
6. Sedation, analgesia and withdrawal

Common drips: fentanyl, morphine, midazolam, dexmedetomidine, ketamine.
After 5 or more days of opioid or benzodiazepine infusions, expect iatrogenic withdrawal. Units use a scoring tool (WAT-1) and a wean plan (for example enteral methadone or lorazepam). Pharmacists often write the wean.
Propofol: long, high dose infusions in children carry risk of propofol infusion syndrome.

7. Everyday pediatric dosing anchors

Acetaminophen 15 mg/kg every 6 hours (max 75 mg/kg/day, not over 4 g/day).
Ibuprofen 10 mg/kg every 6 to 8 hours (6 months and older; max 40 mg/kg/day).
Maintenance fluids: Holliday Segar 4/2/1 rule for rate; AAP 2018 recommends isotonic fluids with appropriate KCl and dextrose for most hospitalized children 28 days to 18 years.
Ondansetron 0.15 mg/kg (max 4 mg per dose in most protocols, 8 mg in some).

8. Pediatric toxicology to know cold

Acetaminophen: NAC (21 hour IV protocol; know St. Mary’s regimen, many sites now use a two bag protocol).
Iron, tricyclics (bicarbonate), button battery (honey or sucralfate before arrival, per guidance), clonidine, sulfonylureas (octreotide).
Poison Control: 1 800 222 1222.

Verify locally at St. Mary’s

Pediatric code sheet or Broselow type system; who prepares drug doses at peds codes.
Standard pediatric drip concentrations in the pump library.
Status epilepticus order set (which second line agent).
DKA order set (two bag system?).
Sedation and withdrawal protocol (WAT-1, wean).

clinical/stroke_core.title: Stroke_Core
clinical/stroke_core.content:
Stroke (Comprehensive Stroke Center): Pharmacist Core
Pharmacist’s job in a stroke alert: confirm weight, check for contraindications (anticoagulants, recent surgery, platelets, glucose), prepare and double check the thrombolytic fast (door to needle goal), manage BP before and after, and set up antithrombotic therapy after.
Sources: AHA/ASA 2026 Guideline for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke (Prabhakaran et al., Stroke, published January 26, 2026); AHA/ASA 2022 Guideline for Spontaneous Intracerebral Hemorrhage; AHA/ASA 2023 Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage Guideline; FDA approval of tenecteplase (TNKase) for acute ischemic stroke (March 2025); Andexxa US market withdrawal (2025).

1. Ischemic stroke: thrombolysis (AHA/ASA 2026)

Tenecteplase is now equally preferred to alteplase (2026). Advantage: a single bolus, fewer mixing and infusion errors.
Time: within 4.5 hours of last known well. Selected patients up to 9 hours based on advanced imaging (2026).
Not for mild, nondisabling symptoms (symptoms that don’t affect daily activities or the ability to work).





















AgentDoseKey safety pointTenecteplase0.25 mg/kg IV bolus over 5 seconds, max 25 mgThe cardiac (STEMI) dose is different and higher. Use the stroke dose only; many sites stock a dedicated stroke kit or dosing chartAlteplase0.9 mg/kg, max 90 mg: 10% as bolus over 1 minute, the rest over 60 minutesAfter the infusion, the dead volume in the tubing must be flushed so the full dose is given [VERIFY St. Mary’s procedure]
Before lytics: BP below 185/110. Glucose checked (treat if below 50; hypoglycemia can mimic stroke). Platelets and INR are not required before starting unless a problem is suspected, but know the contraindications (for example INR above 1.7, platelets below 100,000, therapeutic heparin or enoxaparin, or a recent DOAC dose) [VERIFY 2026 wording on DOACs].
After lytics, for 24 hours: BP below 180/105. No antithrombotics for 24 hours (unless specifically indicated). Neuro checks.
BP agents: labetalol 10 to 20 mg IV over 1 to 2 minutes (may repeat once), nicardipine infusion 5 mg/h titrated by 2.5 mg/h every 5 to 15 minutes (max 15 mg/h), clevidipine 1 to 2 mg/h titrated (max 21 mg/h).
Angioedema after alteplase or tenecteplase (more common with ACE inhibitors): stop the infusion, give methylprednisolone, diphenhydramine and famotidine; epinephrine if it worsens; icatibant or C1 esterase inhibitor may be considered.
Bleeding after a thrombolytic: stop it; cryoprecipitate 10 units, and tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 minutes or aminocaproic acid as an alternative [VERIFY order set].
2. Ischemic stroke: after the acute phase

Minor stroke or high risk TIA: dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin + clopidogrel, 21 days). 2026 update: can be used for NIHSS 4 or 5 (not only 3 or less) and can start within 72 hours.
Load clopidogrel 300 to 600 mg, then 75 mg daily; aspirin 160 to 325 mg load, then 81 mg daily.
Atrial fibrillation: start a DOAC; timing depends on stroke size (ELAN and TIMING trials support earlier starts) [VERIFY 2026 recommendation].
High intensity statin.
Glucose 140 to 180 mg/dL in the hospital.
VTE prophylaxis: enoxaparin or heparin once safe; intermittent pneumatic compression.

3. Intracerebral hemorrhage (AHA/ASA 2022)

BP: for mild to moderate ICH with SBP 150 to 220, lowering to a target of 140 (keeping it in 130 to 150) is reasonable; avoid dropping below 130. Smooth, sustained control (nicardipine or clevidipine drips) matters.
Reversal (the pharmacist’s biggest job here):


































DrugReversalWarfarin4F-PCC (dose by INR and weight per protocol) + vitamin K 10 mg IVDabigatranIdarucizumab 5 g IV (two 2.5 g vials)Apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban4F-PCC 50 units/kg (per protocol). Andexanet alfa was withdrawn from the US market in 2025Heparin infusionProtamine 1 mg per 100 units of heparin given in the last 2 to 3 hours (max 50 mg)EnoxaparinProtamine 1 mg per 1 mg enoxaparin if within 8 hours (0.5 mg per 1 mg if 8 to 12 hours)AntiplateletsPlatelet transfusion is not recommended unless the patient is going to surgery (PATCH trial)

No seizure prophylaxis routinely. Treat hyperglycemia and fever. VTE prophylaxis with heparin or enoxaparin can start 24 to 48 hours after the bleed is stable.

4. Aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (AHA/ASA 2023)

Nimodipine 60 mg orally or by tube every 4 hours for 21 days. Oral only; never IV (deaths have occurred when capsule contents were injected; FDA boxed warning). If BP drops, 30 mg every 2 hours.
BP control before the aneurysm is secured (common target SBP below 160) [VERIFY].
Reversal of any anticoagulant; levetiracetam is preferred over phenytoin if an antiseizure drug is used.

5. Stroke alert checklist (pharmacist)

Weight: measured or estimated? (Tenecteplase dosing is weight banded.)
Last known well time. Anticoagulant, and when was the last dose?
BP below 185/110? If not, have labetalol or nicardipine ready.
Glucose done?
Prepare tenecteplase or alteplase; independent double check of dose and drug (tenecteplase vs alteplase look alike packaging; stroke vs cardiac dose).
Document time of bolus (door to needle).

Verify locally at St. Mary’s

Which thrombolytic St. Mary’s uses for stroke, and the dosing chart.
Stroke alert pharmacist response (does pharmacy go to the ED or CT?).
Anticoagulant reversal order set (4F-PCC dosing method).
Post thrombectomy BP targets in the order set.

clinical/trauma_core.title: Trauma_Core
clinical/trauma_core.content:
Trauma (Level I): Pharmacist Core
Pharmacist’s job in a trauma activation: TXA on time, anticoagulant reversal fast, RSI drugs, antibiotics for open fractures, tetanus, brain injury osmotherapy, and later pain, VTE prophylaxis and withdrawal.
Sources: CRASH-2 (Lancet 2010) and CRASH-3 (Lancet 2019, TBI); ACS TQIP best practice guidelines (massive transfusion; TBI); Brain Trauma Foundation 4th ed. (2016); EAST practice management guidelines (open fracture antibiotics; VTE prophylaxis); CDC tetanus guidance; AHA/ASA 2022 ICH reversal table (Stroke_Core).

1. Tranexamic acid (TXA)

Dose (CRASH-2): 1 g IV over 10 minutes, then 1 g over 8 hours.
Timing: within 3 hours of injury. Benefit is greatest when given early; after 3 hours it may cause harm (CRASH-2 subgroup).
TBI: CRASH-3 showed benefit in mild to moderate TBI when given within 3 hours.
Some EMS systems give 2 g as a single prehospital bolus; check what was already given before ordering more.

Quote it: “CRASH-2: 1 g over 10 minutes then 1 g over 8 hours, and only within 3 hours of injury.”
2. Massive transfusion

Balanced ratio of plasma, platelets and red cells, close to 1:1:1 (PROPPR trial, ACS TQIP).
Calcium: citrate in blood products drops ionized calcium. Expect calcium chloride 1 g IV (central preferred) or calcium gluconate 3 g per protocol, guided by ionized calcium.
Watch potassium (rises with stored blood) and temperature.

3. Anticoagulated trauma patient
Same reversal table as ICH (Stroke_Core section 3). Find out the anticoagulant and the time of the last dose immediately; this is where pharmacists save minutes.
4. Rapid sequence intubation (adult)



































DrugDoseWatchKetamine1 to 2 mg/kg IVGood in hypotension; raises secretionsEtomidate0.3 mg/kg IVAdrenal suppression (single dose)Propofol1 to 2.5 mg/kg IVHypotension: avoid or reduce in shockRocuronium1 to 1.2 mg/kg IVReversal: sugammadex 16 mg/kg for immediate reversalSuccinylcholine1 to 1.5 mg/kg IVAvoid with hyperkalemia, burns or crush injury after 24 to 48 hours, spinal cord injury after the first days, neuromuscular disease, history of malignant hyperthermia
Post intubation: analgesia first (fentanyl), then sedation (propofol, dexmedetomidine). Paralyzed patients must be sedated; rocuronium lasts longer than etomidate.
5. Traumatic brain injury (BTF 2016; ACS TQIP)

Avoid hypotension and hypoxia.
Osmotherapy: mannitol 0.25 to 1 g/kg IV, or hypertonic saline (3% 250 mL, or 23.4% 30 mL central line only, ISMP high alert).
Seizure prophylaxis for severe TBI for 7 days (phenytoin per BTF; levetiracetam is widely used) [VERIFY St. Mary’s choice].
Steroids are not recommended in TBI (CRASH trial).

6. Open fractures (EAST 2022)

Start antibiotics as soon as possible (within 1 hour).
Type I and II: cefazolin 2 g IV (3 g if 120 kg or more).
Type III: cefazolin plus gram negative coverage (for example ceftriaxone, or cefazolin + gentamicin per protocol) [VERIFY order set]. Add penicillin for farm or soil contamination.

7. Tetanus (CDC)

Clean minor wound: Tdap or Td if more than 10 years since last dose.
Dirty or major wound: Tdap or Td if more than 5 years; plus tetanus immune globulin 250 units IM if vaccination history is unknown or fewer than 3 doses.

8. After the trauma bay

VTE prophylaxis: enoxaparin (commonly 30 mg every 12 hours or 40 mg daily, weight and anti Xa adjusted per protocol) once bleeding risk allows, often within 24 to 48 hours (EAST, ACS TQIP) [VERIFY protocol].
Pain: multimodal (acetaminophen, NSAIDs if no bleeding or kidney concern, regional anesthesia, ketamine, opioids). Rib fractures benefit from regional blocks and scheduled nonopioids.
Alcohol withdrawal: CIWA based benzodiazepines or phenobarbital protocols; thiamine before glucose.
Stress ulcer prophylaxis for ventilated or coagulopathic patients.
Burns: Parkland formula, 4 mL/kg per % TBSA of lactated Ringer’s in 24 hours, half in the first 8 hours (from time of burn).
Spinal cord injury: high dose methylprednisolone is not recommended routinely.

Trauma activation checklist (pharmacist)

Weight (estimated) and allergies.
Anticoagulants or antiplatelets? Last dose time?
TXA: injury time? Under 3 hours? Already given by EMS?
RSI kit ready; post intubation sedation.
Open fracture: cefazolin. Tetanus status.
Head injury: hypertonic saline or mannitol ready.

Verify locally at St. Mary’s

Trauma activation pharmacist response.
TXA protocol and EMS doses.
Massive transfusion protocol and calcium replacement.
Open fracture antibiotic order set; VTE prophylaxis protocol for trauma.

curriculum/12_week_plan.title: 12_Week_Plan
curriculum/12_week_plan.content:
12 Week Plan (PGY1 equivalent, self directed)
Built on the ASHP PGY1 competency areas: R1 Patient Care, R2 Practice Advancement, R3 Leadership, R4 Teaching and Education. Each week: 1 module page, 5 daily cases, 1 “quote it” drill, 1 safety alert.
Order is set by risk at St. Mary’s: the specialty areas (NICU, PICU, L&D) and the areas where a PRN pharmacist is alone at night (codes, trauma, stroke, anticoagulation) come first.



















































































WeekModuleWhy nowStatus1LD_Obstetrics_CorePriority area; high alert drugs (magnesium, oxytocin)Built2NICU_CorePriority area; 10 fold error riskBuilt3PICU_CorePriority area; weight based emergenciesBuilt4Codes_Resuscitation (ACLS 2025, PALS 2025, NRP 2025)You may be the only pharmacist at a codeBuilt5Stroke_Core: thrombolysis, BP, reversal, ICHComprehensive stroke centerBuilt6Trauma_Core: TXA, massive transfusion, anticoagulant reversal, RSI, pain and sedationLevel I traumaBuilt7Anticoagulation: heparin, enoxaparin, DOACs, warfarin, HITMost common high alert verificationsBuilt8Infectious Diseases and Stewardship: sepsis, vancomycin AUC, aminoglycosides, beta lactam allergyDaily volumeBuilt9Adult Critical Care: vasopressors, sedation (PADIS), DKA, electrolytesOvernight ICU callsBuilt10IV Room and Sterile Compounding (USP 797, 800), pediatric and neonatal TPNBig at St. Mary’sBuilt11Medication Safety and Regulatory: ISMP high alert list, Joint Commission NPSGs, Florida lawWhat leadership is judged on12Practice Advancement: pick and start one project (see below)What makes you look like a resident
Residency style deliverables (do these and leadership notices)

One medication use evaluation (MUE) or quality project in your first 6 months. Examples: time to TXA in trauma activations, magnesium monitoring compliance on L&D, IV to PO opportunities, vancomycin AUC target attainment. Ask your manager which one helps the department.
One inservice to nurses or pharmacy staff (15 minutes). Example: “Magnesium sulfate toxicity: what the nurse sees first.”
An intervention log. Count and categorize what you catch (dose, duplication, interaction, renal adjustment, allergy). This is the number that proves your value.
Board certification path (later): BCPS is the standard credential that signals residency level knowledge. Florida does not require it; it is optional and a long term goal.

Continuing education priorities

ASHP Midyear (December) and ASHP Summer Meetings; FSHP (Florida Society of Health System Pharmacists) annual meeting.
Florida license renewal CE, including the required medication error and controlled substance hours [VERIFY current Florida Board of Pharmacy rule].
PALS and ACLS provider courses are worth taking even if not required for your role. They give you the code language the teams use.

curriculum/daily_routine.title: Daily_Routine
curriculum/daily_routine.content:
Daily and Shift Routine
The pharmacist workup (use for every order you verify that is not routine)
Based on the JCPP Pharmacists’ Patient Care Process: Collect, Assess, Plan, Implement, Follow up.

Who: age, weight (dosing weight for peds and neonates, in kg only), height, allergies with reaction type, pregnancy or lactation status.
Why: indication. If you can’t name it, ask.
Organs: SCr and CrCl or eGFR, urine output, LFTs, platelets and INR for anticoagulants.
Drug check: dose, route, frequency, duration, max dose, concentration, compatibility, duplication, interactions, high alert status.
Monitor: what level, lab or vital sign tells you it is working or hurting, and when.
Communicate: if you call, use SBAR: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation. End with a specific recommendation and a guideline you can name.

How to sound like a resident on the phone

“Dr. ___, this is Shallanda, the pharmacist. I’m calling about [patient] in [room]. The [drug] order is [dose]; with a CrCl of 28, the [source, year] recommends [change]. Would you like me to adjust it to [specific order]?”

Name the source and year. Give the exact order. Let them say yes.
Daily 20 minutes

1 case from Cases_LD_NICU_PICU, timed, out loud.
1 item from ISMP or FDA (see Stay_Current).

Weekly 2 hours

1 module page, then the “Verify locally” list for that module at work.
