drug-hub/antimicrobial_guide.content:
Antimicrobial Guide (empiric regimens by infection, adults)
Her own quick guide, built from public guideline summaries. Normal kidney function doses; adjust for CrCl. Always check St. Mary’s antibiogram and order sets first, and narrow once cultures return.
Key: ✅✅ two independent sources · ✅ one source · ⚠️ [VERIFY] · Background: ID_Core

Pneumonia



























































SituationRegimenDurationCheckCAP, inpatient, not severe, no MRSA or Pseudomonas riskCeftriaxone 1 to 2 g IV daily (or ampicillin sulbactam 1.5 to 3 g q6h) plus azithromycin 500 mg daily; or levofloxacin 750 mg daily or moxifloxacin 400 mg daily aloneAt least 5 days and clinically stable✅✅ [1][2]CAP, macrolide and fluoroquinolone both contraindicatedBeta lactam above plus doxycycline 100 mg BID✅✅ [1][2]CAP, severeBeta lactam plus azithromycin, or beta lactam plus levofloxacin or moxifloxacin✅✅ [1][2]CAP with MRSA risk (prior respiratory MRSA, or IV antibiotics and hospitalization in 90 days, locally validated)Add vancomycin (AUC dosed) or linezolid 600 mg q12h✅✅ [1][2]CAP with Pseudomonas riskPiperacillin tazobactam 4.5 g q6h, cefepime 2 g q8h, ceftazidime 2 g q8h, meropenem 1 g q8h, imipenem 500 mg q6h, or aztreonam 2 g q8h✅✅ [1][2]HAP, no high riskOne of: piperacillin tazobactam 4.5 g q6h, cefepime 2 g q8h, levofloxacin 750 mg daily, meropenem 1 g q8h7 days✅✅ [3][4]HAP with Pseudomonas risk or high mortality (shock, ventilator)Two antipseudomonal agents from different classes (beta lactam plus fluoroquinolone or aminoglycoside) ± MRSA coverage7 days✅ [3]HAP MRSA coverageWhen IV antibiotics in 90 days or local MRSA above 20% (or unknown). Vancomycin or linezolid 600 mg q12h. Stop vancomycin if MRSA nares negative and cultures don’t grow MRSA✅ [3][4]
Steroids are not routine for CAP or influenza pneumonia; they follow the sepsis guideline for refractory shock ✅ [1].
Urinary tract (2025 IDSA complicated UTI)









































SituationRegimenDurationCheckcUTI or pyelonephritis, no sepsisCeftriaxone 2 g IV daily, a fluoroquinolone (avoid if used in past 12 months), or TMP SMX by susceptibility7 days (5 to 7 with a fluoroquinolone)✅✅ [5][6]SepsisThird or fourth generation cephalosporin, piperacillin tazobactam, carbapenem or fluoroquinolone; ertapenem if prior ESBL7 days, including bacteremia✅✅ [5][6]Don’t use for cUTINitrofurantoin, oral fosfomycin (low kidney and blood levels)✅ [5]Oral step downOnce improving and susceptible: levofloxacin, TMP SMX DS BID, cephalexin 1 g TID, amoxicillin clavulanate✅✅ [5][6]Positive culture, no symptomsDon’t treat✅ [6]
Skin and soft tissue









































SituationRegimenDurationCheckNonpurulent cellulitis, mild (oral)Cephalexin 500 mg QID (or 1 g q8h) or cefadroxilAbout 5 days (5 to 7)✅✅ [7][8]Nonpurulent, moderate to severe (IV)Cefazolin 2 g IV q8h5 to 7 days✅ [8]AbscessIncision and drainage first. Antibiotics if over 2 cm or high risk: TMP SMX DS 1 to 2 tabs BID or doxycycline 100 mg BID5 days✅✅ [7][8]Severe, septic or MRSAVancomycin (AUC dosed), linezolid 600 mg q12h, or daptomycin✅ [8]Necrotizing infectionSurgical emergency; broad coverage plus clindamycin for toxin suppression ⚠️ [VERIFY]⚠️
Meningitis (adults)








































SituationRegimenCheckEmpiric, age 18 to 50Vancomycin 15 to 20 mg/kg q8 to 12h plus ceftriaxone 2 g IV q12h✅ [9] ⚠️ [VERIFY second source]Age over 50, pregnant or immunocompromisedAdd ampicillin 2 g IV q4h (Listeria)✅ [9]Severe beta lactam allergyReplace ceftriaxone with moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily (keep vancomycin)✅ [9]Dexamethasone0.15 mg/kg (about 10 mg) IV q6h for 2 to 4 days, started 10 to 20 minutes before or with the first antibiotic; not after antibiotics have started; continue only if pneumococcal✅✅ [9][10]Suspected HSVAcyclovir 10 mg/kg IV q8h✅ [9]Neonates and childrenSee NICU_Core and PICU_Core
C. difficile
Fidaxomicin 200 mg PO BID x 10 days, or vancomycin 125 mg PO QID x 10 days ✅✅ (see ID_Core).
Surgical prophylaxis
Cefazolin 2 g IV (3 g if 120 kg or more) within 60 minutes before incision ⚠️ [VERIFY ASHP 2013 guideline]. See Trauma_Core for open fractures.

drug-hub/monographs/4f_pcc.content:
4 Factor Prothrombin Complex Concentrate (4F-PCC, Kcentra) · Drug Monograph
Drug Monographs section. Built from public sources. Confirm against St. Mary’s anticoagulant reversal order set.
Key: ✅✅ two independent sources · ✅ one source · ⚠️ [VERIFY]
Boxed warning: arterial and venous thromboembolic events. Not studied in patients with a thromboembolic event in the prior 3 months ✅ [1].
Warfarin reversal (labeled use), with vitamin K

































Pre treatment INRDose (units of factor IX per kg)MaxCheckSources2 to below 425 units/kg2,500 units✅✅[1] label; [2] Children’s Mercy guideline4 to 635 units/kg3,500 units✅✅[1][2]above 650 units/kg5,000 units✅✅[1][2]

Dose by weight up to 100 kg; don’t exceed the max above 100 kg ✅ [1].
Give vitamin K at the same time (4F-PCC wears off before warfarin does) ✅✅ [1][2]. Adult major bleeding: vitamin K 10 mg IV ✅ (AHA/ASA ICH 2022, see Stroke_Core).
Infusion: 0.12 mL/kg/min (about 3 units/kg/min), max 8.4 mL/min ✅ [1].
Repeat dosing is not recommended by the label ✅ [1].
Check INR about 30 minutes after the infusion ✅ [2].

Factor Xa inhibitor bleeding (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban), off label

4F-PCC 50 units/kg per many protocols (some use fixed doses such as 2,000 units) ⚠️ [VERIFY St. Mary’s protocol].
Andexanet alfa was withdrawn from the US market in 2025, so 4F-PCC is the main option ✅ (see Stroke_Core).
Dabigatran: idarucizumab 5 g IV is the specific reversal agent ✅ (see Stroke_Core).

Pharmacist checklist

Which anticoagulant, and when was the last dose?
Current INR and weight (cap at 100 kg).
Vitamin K ordered with it for warfarin.
Any thrombosis in the last 3 months? Weigh the risk.
INR 30 minutes after; no routine repeat dose.

Sources

Kcentra prescribing information (Drugs.com)
Children’s Mercy Kansas City: Warfarin antidotes clinical practice guideline

drug-hub/monographs/enoxaparin.title: Enoxaparin
drug-hub/monographs/enoxaparin.content:
Enoxaparin (Lovenox) · Drug Monograph
Drug Monographs section (does the job of a general drug reference such as Lexicomp or Micromedex). Built from public sources. Confirm against St. Mary’s protocol and the hospital’s drug reference before clinical use.
Verification key: ✅✅ confirmed in two independent sources · ✅ one source · ⚠️ [VERIFY] not yet confirmed twice. Two versions of the same FDA label count as one source.
ISMP High Alert Medication (anticoagulant). Boxed warning: spinal and epidural hematoma with neuraxial anesthesia or spinal puncture, which can cause permanent paralysis ✅✅ [1][2].

Adult dosing (SC unless noted)




































































IndicationDoseCrCl below 30 mL/minCheckSourcesMedical VTE prophylaxis40 mg once daily30 mg once daily✅✅[1][2]Abdominal surgery prophylaxis40 mg once daily, first dose 2 h before surgery30 mg once daily✅[1]Hip or knee replacement30 mg every 12 h starting 12 to 24 h after surgery (hip alternative: 40 mg daily)30 mg once daily✅[1]DVT or PE treatment1 mg/kg every 12 h, or 1.5 mg/kg once daily (inpatient)1 mg/kg once daily✅✅[1][2]Unstable angina / NSTEMI1 mg/kg every 12 h with aspirin1 mg/kg once daily✅✅[1][2]STEMI, under 75 years30 mg IV bolus + 1 mg/kg SC, then 1 mg/kg every 12 h (max 100 mg for the first 2 doses)30 mg IV bolus + 1 mg/kg, then 1 mg/kg once daily✅✅[1][2]STEMI, 75 years or olderNo IV bolus. 0.75 mg/kg every 12 h (max 75 mg for the first 2 doses)1 mg/kg once daily, no bolus✅✅[1][2]STEMI going to PCILast SC dose under 8 h before balloon: nothing extra. Over 8 h: 0.3 mg/kg IV bolus✅[1]

CrCl 30 to 80 mL/min: no dose change, but watch closely for bleeding ✅ [1].
Low body weight (women under 45 kg, men under 57 kg): higher exposure on fixed prophylaxis doses; watch for bleeding ✅ [1].
Obesity (BMI over 30): no consensus on prophylaxis dose adjustment per the label ✅ [1]. Know St. Mary’s obesity protocol ⚠️ [VERIFY].

Monitoring

PT and aPTT do not measure enoxaparin effect ✅ [1].
Anti Xa is used in renal impairment, obesity, pregnancy, children or bleeding ✅✅ [1][2].
Anti Xa targets (treatment): draw a peak about 4 hours after the dose, after the 3rd dose (steady state) ✅✅ [2][3].

1 mg/kg every 12 h: peak 0.5 to 1.0 units/mL ✅ [3]
1.5 mg/kg once daily: peak 1.0 to 2.0 units/mL ✅ [3]
Confirm St. Mary’s lab ranges ⚠️ [VERIFY]


Platelets (HIT risk is lower than with heparin but present), hemoglobin, SCr.

Neuraxial timing (epidural, spinal, catheter)

Prophylactic dose: wait at least 12 hours after the dose before placement or removal ✅✅ [2][4].
Treatment dose (1 mg/kg every 12 h or 1.5 mg/kg daily): wait at least 24 hours ✅✅ [2][4].
After catheter removal: next dose no sooner than 4 hours later ✅ [2].
ASRA updated its guideline after the 2010 edition cited here; check the current edition and St. Mary’s anesthesia policy ⚠️ [VERIFY].

Reversal (protamine)

Enoxaparin given within 8 hours: 1 mg protamine per 1 mg enoxaparin ✅✅ [1][2].
More than 8 hours, or a second dose needed: 0.5 mg per 1 mg ✅ [1].
12 hours or more since the dose: protamine may not be needed ✅ [1].
Protamine reverses only about 60% of anti Xa activity ✅✅ [1][2].
Max 50 mg per dose ✅ [2]. Risk of hypotension and anaphylactoid reactions; give slowly with resuscitation available ✅ [1].

Contraindications
Active major bleeding; immune mediated HIT within the past 100 days or circulating antibodies; hypersensitivity to enoxaparin, heparin or pork products; benzyl alcohol allergy (multiple dose vials) ✅ [1].
Pediatrics and neonates
Not FDA approved for neonates or infants, though it is used off label with anti Xa monitoring. Multiple dose vials contain benzyl alcohol (gasping syndrome); use single dose syringes ✅ [1]. Pediatric dosing ⚠️ [VERIFY against the pediatric dosing reference St. Mary’s uses].
Pharmacist verification checklist

Indication matches the dose (prophylaxis vs treatment vs ACS).
Weight and CrCl (Cockcroft Gault) both current.
Age 75 or older with STEMI: no bolus, 0.75 mg/kg.
Epidural or spinal planned or in place? Check timing.
Heparin running or given recently? Avoid double anticoagulation.
Platelets, hemoglobin, anti Xa plan if renal, obese or pregnant.

Sources (open these to verify)

FDA label, Lovenox (Sanofi, revised 05/2025) · earlier version on Drugs@FDA (2021)
Jupalli A, Iqbal AM. Enoxaparin. StatPearls (updated Aug 2023)
University of Michigan Medical Laboratories: LMWH anti Xa test
Pharmacy Times: Neuraxial anesthesia and anticoagulation (summarizes ASRA 3rd edition, Horlocker et al., Reg Anesth Pain Med 2010;35:64)

Pyrls: search “enoxaparin” in Drug Summaries.

drug-hub/monographs/gentamicin.content:
Gentamicin (IV) · Drug Monograph
Drug Monographs section. Built from public sources. Confirm against St. Mary’s aminoglycoside protocol.
Key: ✅✅ two independent sources · ✅ one source · ⚠️ [VERIFY]
Boxed warning: nephrotoxicity, usually irreversible ototoxicity (vestibular and hearing), neuromuscular blockade; avoid other nephrotoxic or neurotoxic drugs and potent loop diuretics; fetal harm ✅ [1].
Adult dosing



























































ApproachDoseCheckSourcesTraditional (label)3 mg/kg/day divided every 8 h; up to 5 mg/kg/day for life threatening infection, then back to 3✅[1]Traditional targetsAvoid peaks above 12 mcg/mL and troughs above 2 mcg/mL✅[1]Renal (label method)Interval (h) ≈ SCr × 8, or divide dose by SCr for every 8 h dosing✅[1]Hemodialysis1 to 1.7 mg/kg after dialysis✅[1]Extended interval (Hartford)7 mg/kg; one random level; plot on the nomogram for every 24, 36 or 48 h✅✅[2] Nicolau 1995; [3] nomogram guideHartford rulesOnly valid for 7 mg/kg; assumes Vd 0.3 L/kg; level above the q48h zone means switch to traditional dosing; on a line, pick the longer interval✅[3]Level timing for Hartford6 to 14 h after the start of the dose⚠️[VERIFY original paper]Weight for dosingActual weight, or adjusted weight in obesity per protocol⚠️[VERIFY St. Mary’s]
Pediatrics and neonates (label)

Neonates 1 week old or younger: 2.5 mg/kg every 12 h. Infants: 2.5 mg/kg every 8 h. Children: 2 to 2.5 mg/kg every 8 h ✅ [1].
Most NICUs use extended interval dosing by gestational and postnatal age instead (see NICU_Core) ⚠️ [VERIFY unit chart].

Pharmacist checklist

Which method: traditional or extended interval?
Weight (actual vs adjusted), SCr and urine output.
Level ordered at the right time.
Avoid with other nephrotoxins where possible; baseline hearing complaints.
Duration: label usual 7 to 10 days ✅ [1].

drug-hub/monographs/heparin.content:
Heparin (unfractionated) · Drug Monograph
Drug Monographs section (does the job of a general drug reference such as Lexicomp or Micromedex). Built from public sources. Confirm against St. Mary’s protocol and the hospital’s drug reference before clinical use.
Verification key: ✅✅ confirmed in two independent sources · ✅ one source · ⚠️ [VERIFY] not yet confirmed twice
ISMP High Alert Medication. Independent double check per St. Mary’s policy.

Quick card



















































































ItemValueCheckSourcesVTE treatment (weight based)80 units/kg IV bolus, then 18 units/kg/h; adjust by nomogram✅✅[1] Raschke 1993; [2] WikEM summary of StatPearlsACS (NSTE-ACS, STEMI with fibrinolysis)60 units/kg bolus (max 4,000 units), then 12 units/kg/h (max 1,000 units/h)✅✅[3] ESC/ACC/AHA dosing as summarized by Termedia review; [4] hospital ACS heparin order set (Southern Health)PCI70 to 100 units/kg bolus (50 to 70 units/kg with a GP IIb/IIIa inhibitor), ACT guided⚠️[3] gives 100 units/kg (60 with GP IIb/IIIa) [VERIFY current ACC/AHA PCI wording]VTE prophylaxis5,000 units SC every 8 to 12 hours⚠️[VERIFY CHEST prophylaxis guideline]Label continuous infusion (fixed dosing)5,000 unit IV bolus, then 20,000 to 40,000 units/24 h✅[5] FDA label (DailyMed)Monitoring targetaPTT 1.5 to 2 times control (label) or per hospital anti Xa range✅[5] label; anti Xa 0.3 to 0.7 units/mL commonly used ⚠️ [VERIFY St. Mary’s]Monitoring timingaPTT 6 hours after bolus and after each rate change, then daily when therapeutic✅[4]PlateletsCheck periodically; stop if below 100,000 or new thrombosis (suspect HIT)✅[5]PotassiumHeparin can raise K (aldosterone suppression); check if at risk or therapy over 5 days✅[5]ReversalProtamine about 1 mg per 100 units of heparin given (consider heparin’s 30 to 90 minute half life); max 50 mg in any 10 minutes✅✅[5] label; [6] premixed heparin label (Baxter)Neonates and infantsUse preservative free heparin (benzyl alcohol causes gasping syndrome)✅[5]Pediatric treatment dosingLoad 75 to 100 units/kg, then about 28 units/kg/h (infants) or 20 units/kg/h (over 1 year)⚠️[VERIFY CHEST pediatric antithrombotic guideline and St. Mary’s pediatric protocol]
Safety (why it’s high alert)

Look alike strengths: 1,000, 5,000 and 10,000 units/mL vials look alike. Fatal pediatric hemorrhages have happened when 1 mL heparin vials were confused with 1 mL catheter lock flush vials (FDA label section 5.1) ✅ [5].
Use premixed bags and smart pump libraries for infusions.
Contraindicated with a history of HIT, uncontrolled active bleeding (except DIC), and when coagulation tests can’t be done at appropriate intervals ✅ [5].

Heparin induced thrombocytopenia (HIT)

Use the 4Ts score to estimate pretest probability; with a low 4Ts score, don’t send HIT testing and don’t treat empirically (strong recommendation) ✅ [7] ASH 2018.
If HIT is suspected (intermediate or high 4Ts): stop all heparin (including flushes and heparin coated catheters) and start a non heparin anticoagulant: argatroban, bivalirudin, fondaparinux or a DOAC (conditional) ✅ [7].
Argatroban: 2 mcg/kg/min; 0.5 mcg/kg/min in moderate or severe hepatic impairment; max 10 mcg/kg/min; aPTT 1.5 to 3 times baseline (not above 100 seconds), check 2 hours after starting or changing ✅ [8] FDA label.
Warfarin overlap with argatroban: no loading dose; stop argatroban when INR is above 4 on combined therapy (at argatroban 2 mcg/kg/min or less), recheck INR in 4 to 6 hours ✅ [8].
Start warfarin only after platelets recover (commonly at least 150,000) ⚠️ [VERIFY ASH 2018 full text].

Pharmacist verification checklist

Indication and the right nomogram (VTE vs ACS vs low intensity).
Dosing weight (actual body weight; know St. Mary’s cap for obesity).
Baseline aPTT or anti Xa, CBC, platelets, SCr.
Any enoxaparin in the last 12 hours? (Don’t bolus) ✅ [4]
Concentration and bag match the pump library.
Lab draw times ordered.

drug-hub/monographs/insulin_iv_dka.title: Insulin_IV_DKA
drug-hub/monographs/insulin_iv_dka.content:
Insulin, IV (DKA and HHS, adults) · Drug Monograph
Drug Monographs section. Built from public sources. Confirm against St. Mary’s DKA order set before clinical use.
Key: ✅✅ two independent sources · ✅ one source · ⚠️ [VERIFY]
ISMP High Alert Medication. Use the standard concentration in the smart pump library and an independent double check.
DKA diagnosis (2024 consensus)
All three: D glucose 200 mg/dL or higher, or known diabetes at any glucose (catches euglycemic DKA on SGLT2 inhibitors); K beta hydroxybutyrate 3.0 mmol/L or higher (or urine ketones 2+); A pH below 7.3 and/or bicarbonate below 18 ✅✅ [1][2].
Dosing



























































ItemRecommendationCheckSourcesSevere DKAFixed rate IV regular insulin 0.1 units/kg/h; no routine bolus (0.1 units/kg bolus only if IV access is delayed)✅✅[1][2]HHS0.05 units/kg/h (treat as DKA if ketotic or acidotic)✅✅[1][2]Potassium below 3.5Hold insulin. Give potassium about 10 mmol/h until K is above 3.5✅✅[1][2]Potassium 3.5 to 5.0Add 10 to 20 mmol K per liter of fluid; goal K 4 to 5✅✅[1][2]Potassium above 5.0No potassium; recheck every 2 h✅[1]Glucose below 250Add D5 or D10; lower DKA insulin to 0.05 units/kg/h; keep insulin running until ketones clear✅✅[1][2]Glucose goal during DKA treatment150 to 200 mg/dL (HHS 200 to 250)✅[1]Mild or uncomplicated moderate DKASC rapid acting insulin every 1 to 2 h is an accepted alternative✅✅[1][2]
Change from older teaching: the 2009 statement used K 3.3 as the cutoff and allowed a 0.1 units/kg bolus. The 2024 consensus uses 3.5 and no routine bolus ✅ [1]. Pediatric DKA follows ISPAD 2022 (see PICU_Core).
Fluids
Isotonic saline or balanced crystalloid 500 to 1,000 mL/h for 2 to 4 h if heart and kidneys allow; smaller boluses in older adults and heart or kidney failure ✅ [1].
Resolution and transition

DKA resolved: beta hydroxybutyrate below 0.6 mmol/L and pH 7.3 or higher or bicarbonate 18 or higher ✅ [1].
Give basal insulin at least 1 to 2 hours before stopping the drip ✅✅ [1][2]. Estimate total daily dose 0.3 to 0.6 units/kg/day ✅✅ [1][2].

Monitoring
K at baseline, 2 h after insulin starts, then every 4 h; glucose hourly ✅ [1].
Pharmacist checklist

K result before insulin starts.
No bolus unless IV delay.
Dextrose added at glucose below 250.
SGLT2 inhibitor on home list? Hold it.
Basal insulin ordered 1 to 2 h before the drip stops.

Sources

Rodriguez Alvarez P, et al. Hyperglycemic crises in adults: a look at the 2024 consensus report. Cleve Clin J Med. 2025;92(3):152-158. Summarizes Umpierrez GE, et al. Diabetes Care. 2024;47(8):1257-1275 (doi:10.2337/dci24-0032).
Cleveland Clinic Consult QD: Hyperglycemic crises in adults, the 2024 consensus report

drug-hub/monographs/magnesium_sulfate.content:
Magnesium Sulfate (IV) · Drug Monograph
Drug Monographs section. Built from public sources. Confirm against St. Mary’s L&D magnesium order set.
Key: ✅✅ two independent sources · ✅ one source · ⚠️ [VERIFY]
ISMP High Alert Medication (IV magnesium). Use premixed bags and a dedicated pump channel.
Preeclampsia and eclampsia





















































ItemDoseCheckSourcesLoading dose4 to 6 g IV over 15 to 20 minutes✅✅[1] label (over 15 min); [2] UT Southwestern 2026 (over 15 to 20 min)Maintenance1 to 2 g/h by pump✅✅[1][2]IM option10 g (5 g each buttock), then 5 g IM every 4 h✅[2]Recurrent seizure on magnesiumExtra 2 g IV✅✅[1][2]Daily maximum30 to 40 g per 24 h✅[1]Duration24 h after delivery or last seizure; label: do not use beyond 5 to 7 days (fetal hypocalcemia, bone demineralization, neonatal fractures)✅✅[1][2]Severe renal impairment or oliguria4 g load, then 1 g/h, max 20 g per 48 h; check serum levels✅[1]
Monitoring and toxicity

Check patellar reflexes, respiratory rate (concern below about 16 per label), urine output (keep at least 100 mL per 4 h; stop if lower, especially with rising SCr), serum magnesium ✅✅ [1][2].
Label levels: reflexes weaken above about 4 mEq/L; respiratory paralysis risk at about 10 mEq/L ✅ [1]. Eclampsia target per label 2.5 to 5 mEq/L (3 to 6 mg/dL) ✅ [1].
Antidote: stop the infusion; calcium gluconate 1 g (10 mL of 10%) IV over about 3 minutes; support breathing. Have calcium at the bedside before starting ✅✅ [1][2].
Contraindications: heart block or myocardial damage, myasthenia gravis ✅ [1]. Don’t combine with nifedipine or terbutaline per label caution ✅ [1].
Newborns of treated mothers may need resuscitation and calcium ✅ [1].

Other uses (not in the preeclampsia label)

Torsades de pointes or hypomagnesemic arrest: 1 to 2 g IV ✅ (see Codes_Resuscitation).
Fetal neuroprotection before 32 weeks: per L&D protocol ⚠️ [VERIFY].
Hypomagnesemia repletion: per St. Mary’s electrolyte protocol ⚠️ [VERIFY].

Sources

FDA label, Magnesium Sulfate in 5% Dextrose Injection (Hospira, rev. 4/2019)

drug-hub/monographs/norepinephrine.content:
Norepinephrine · Drug Monograph
Drug Monographs section. Built from public sources. Confirm against St. Mary’s vasopressor titration protocol and pump library.
Key: ✅✅ two independent sources · ✅ one source · ⚠️ [VERIFY]

ItemRecommendationCheckSourcesRole in septic shockFirst line vasopressor✅✅[2] SSC 2021; [3] SSC summaryMAP target65 mmHg✅✅[2][3]Label starting rate8 to 12 mcg/min, then titrate; usual maintenance 2 to 4 mcg/min✅[1]Weight based dosing (mcg/kg/min)Many ICUs use it⚠️[VERIFY St. Mary’s units]Add vasopressinWhen MAP is inadequate on low to moderate norepinephrine✅[2]Peripheral startReasonable short term in a proximal vein above the antecubital fossa while central access is placed✅[2]Cardiac dysfunction with poor perfusionConsider adding dobutamine or switching to epinephrine✅[2]ExtravasationPhentolamine 5 to 10 mg in 10 to 15 mL NS, infiltrated into the area as soon as possible (works best within 12 h)✅[1]Premixed bags4 mg/250 mL (16 mcg/mL), 8 mg/250 mL (32 mcg/mL), 16 mg/250 mL (64 mcg/mL) in NS✅[1]Infusion siteLarge vein; avoid leg veins in elderly or vascular disease✅[1]
Drip math
At 16 mcg/mL, 5 mcg/min = 0.31 mL/min = about 18.8 mL/h. (See Codes_Resuscitation and IV prep notes.)

Concentration matches the pump library entry.
Units: mcg/min vs mcg/kg/min.
Line: central, or peripheral with a time limit and site checks.
Phentolamine available.

ISMP High Alert Medication (concentrated potassium). Never give IV push. Use premixed bags; concentrated vials are kept out of patient care areas per ISMP practice ⚠️ [VERIFY St. Mary’s storage policy].
Rates and limits















































ItemLimitCheckSourcesUsual maximum rate10 mEq/h (serum K above 2.5)✅✅[1] label; [2] StatPearlsAbove 10 mEq/hCentral line with continuous cardiac monitoring✅✅[1][2]Urgent (K below 2.0 with ECG changes or paralysis)Up to 40 mEq/h with continuous ECG and frequent K checks✅[1]Usual maximum per 24 h200 mEq (400 mEq urgent, monitored)✅[1]40 mEq/100 mL (400 mEq/L) bagCentral line only✅[1]Common hospital central rate limit20 mEq/h⚠️[VERIFY St. Mary’s policy]

About 20 mEq IV raises serum K by roughly 0.25 mEq/L ✅ [2].
Use only with a calibrated infusion pump; confirm catheter placement ✅ [1].
Extravasation causes severe tissue injury ✅ [1].
Check magnesium too: low magnesium makes hypokalemia hard to correct ⚠️ [VERIFY second source].

Rate at or below 10 mEq/h peripherally.
Central line and telemetry for anything faster.
Renal function and urine output before repleting.
Not running with other potassium sources (TPN, maintenance fluids) without a total count.

drug-hub/monographs/thrombolytics_stroke.content:
Tenecteplase and Alteplase (acute ischemic stroke) · Drug Monograph
Drug Monographs section. Built from public sources. Confirm against St. Mary’s stroke alert order set.
Key: ✅✅ two independent sources · ✅ one source · ⚠️ [VERIFY]
ISMP High Alert Medication (thrombolytics). Look alike names and packaging: alteplase vs tenecteplase, and stroke dose vs cardiac dose.
Dosing





























AgentStroke doseCheckSourcesTenecteplase0.25 mg/kg actual body weight, max 25 mg, single IV bolus over 5 seconds, then NS flush (not dextrose compatible)✅✅[1] SUNY Downstate pharmacy update 2025; [2] AHA/ASA 2026 summary; FDA approval for stroke March 2025 [3]Tenecteplase cardiac (STEMI) bands, for contrastunder 60 kg 30 mg; 60 to 69 kg 35 mg; 70 to 79 kg 40 mg; 80 to 89 kg 45 mg; 90 kg or more 50 mg✅[1]Alteplase0.9 mg/kg, max 90 mg: 10% bolus over 1 minute, the rest over 60 minutes✅✅[1]; [4] Stroke module sources
2026 AHA/ASA guideline: tenecteplase is equally preferred to alteplase; window up to 4.5 h, or up to 9 h in selected patients by imaging ✅✅ [2][5].
Key contraindications (bleeding risk)
Prior or current intracranial hemorrhage; ischemic stroke, head trauma or intracranial surgery within 3 months; SAH; GI bleed or GI cancer within 21 days; aortic dissection; endocarditis; platelets below 100,000; INR above 1.7; treatment dose enoxaparin within 24 h; recent DOAC; heparin with aPTT above 40 s ✅ [1]. (Full list: St. Mary’s order set.)
Around the dose

BP below 185/110 before; below 180/105 for 24 h after ✅ (see Stroke_Core).
No antithrombotics for 24 h after.
Angioedema and bleeding management: see Stroke_Core.

Pharmacist checklist

Which agent? Read the vial name twice.
Weight: measured or estimated; stroke dose, not cardiac.
Tenecteplase: draw up only the stroke dose and discard the rest per policy.
Anticoagulant history and last dose time.
Document bolus time.

Key: ✅✅ two independent sources · ✅ one source · ⚠️ [VERIFY]
Dosing and monitoring (2020 ASHP/IDSA/PIDS/SIDP consensus, serious MRSA)

































































ItemRecommendationCheckSourcesTargetAUC 400 to 600 mg·h/L (assuming MIC 1)✅✅[1][2]Trough only monitoringNot recommended✅✅[1][2]How to get AUCBayesian software (preferred) or two levels (one 1 to 2 h after infusion, one trough)✅✅[1][2]Loading dose (critically ill)20 to 35 mg/kg actual body weight, max 3,000 mg✅✅[1][2]Pediatrics 3 months to 12 years60 to 80 mg/kg/day divided every 6 h; same AUC target✅[1]Pediatrics 12 years and older60 to 70 mg/kg/day divided every 6 to 8 h✅[1]Pediatric empiric max3,600 mg/day (normal kidneys)✅[1]Maintenance (adults)Usually 15 to 20 mg/kg every 8 to 12 h, then adjust to AUC⚠️[VERIFY full guideline]NeonatesAUC guided where possible; use the neonatal dosing reference⚠️see NICU_Core
Safety

Higher AUC (above 600) and troughs above 15 to 20 raise acute kidney injury risk; watch with piperacillin tazobactam, contrast, loop diuretics ⚠️ [VERIFY second source].
Vancomycin infusion reaction (formerly “red man syndrome”): slow the infusion (commonly at least 60 minutes per 1 g); antihistamine. It’s not a true allergy ⚠️ [VERIFY label rate].

Pharmacist checklist

Indication and whether a loading dose is needed.
Actual body weight; SCr trend; urine output.
Level plan (Bayesian or two levels), not trough only.
Nephrotoxic combinations.
Infusion time matches dose.

journal-club/jc_act.title: JC_AcT
journal-club/jc_act.content:
Journal Club: AcT (tenecteplase vs alteplase for stroke)
Key: ✅✅ two independent sources · ✅ one source · ⚠️ [VERIFY] · Template: Journal_Club_Template · Module: Stroke_Core · Drug: Thrombolytics_Stroke
0. 60 second bottom line

“AcT (Lancet 2022) randomized 1,600 thrombolysis eligible stroke patients within 4.5 hours at 22 Canadian centers to tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg (max 25 mg) or alteplase 0.9 mg/kg. Excellent outcome (mRS 0 to 1 at 90 to 120 days) was 36.9% vs 34.8% (difference 2.1%, 95% CI minus 2.6 to 6.9), meeting the minus 5% noninferiority margin. Symptomatic ICH (3.4% vs 3.2%) and death (15.3% vs 15.4%) were similar. The main limitation is open label treatment. For our patients, tenecteplase is a one bolus option with the same results, and the dose must be the stroke dose, not the cardiac dose.” ✅✅ [1][2]

1. Citation and context
Menon BK, Buck BH, Singh N, et al. Lancet 2022 (published online June 28). ✅✅ [1][2] Volume and pages ⚠️ [VERIFY]. Pragmatic, registry linked.
2. PICO





























PopulationAdults 18 or older, ischemic stroke within 4.5 h, eligible for thrombolysis; mean age 74, 48% female ✅ [1]InterventionTenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg IV bolus, max 25 mg ✅✅ [1][2]ComparatorAlteplase 0.9 mg/kg, max 90 mg (10% bolus, 90% over 60 min) ✅✅ [1][2]OutcomesPrimary: mRS 0 to 1 at 90 to 120 days. Safety: symptomatic ICH at 24 h, 90 day deathDesignNoninferiority, open label, blinded outcome assessment, margin minus 5% ✅✅ [1][2]
3. Validity

Strengths: real world, large, blinded outcome assessors, both ITT style and safety analyses.
Red flags: open label; telephone outcome assessment; few primary stroke centers; daytime only enrollment at some sites ✅ [2].
Noninferiority check: margin stated and met; the whole CI sits above minus 5%.

4. Results

































OutcomeTenecteplaseAlteplaseEffectCheckmRS 0 to 136.9% (296/802)34.8% (266/765)Difference 2.1% (minus 2.6 to 6.9)✅✅ [1][2]Symptomatic ICH, 24 h3.4%3.2%Similar✅✅ [1][2]90 day death15.3%15.4%Similar✅ [2]
5. Applicability at St. Mary’s
Single bolus helps with transfers and drip and ship. Our biggest risk is the dose: tenecteplase cardiac (STEMI) dosing uses weight bands up to 50 mg. See Thrombolytics_Stroke.
6. Role in therapy
“For eligible ischemic stroke within 4.5 hours, tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg (max 25 mg) is a reasonable first line alternative to alteplase; AHA/ASA 2026 lists it as equally preferred.”
7. Pharmacist’s angle

Confirm the stroke dose and the max of 25 mg.
Check the weight band chart and the vial.
Same BP and antithrombotic rules as alteplase.

Sources

ACC: AcT trial summary
Calgary EM: AcT trial summary (PDF)

Last verified: 2026-10-17.

journal-club/jc_crash-2.title: JC_CRASH-2
journal-club/jc_crash-2.content:
Journal Club: CRASH-2 (TXA in trauma)
Key: ✅✅ two independent sources · ✅ one source · ⚠️ [VERIFY] · Template: Journal_Club_Template · Module: Trauma_Core
0. 60 second bottom line

“CRASH-2 (Lancet 2010) randomized 20,211 bleeding or at risk adult trauma patients within 8 hours of injury to tranexamic acid 1 g over 10 minutes then 1 g over 8 hours, or placebo. 28 day all cause death was 14.5% vs 16.0% (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.85 to 0.97; ARR 1.5%, NNT 67). The main limitation is that benefit depends on timing: a later analysis found harm when TXA started more than 3 hours after injury. For our trauma patients, TXA goes in within 3 hours or not at all.” ✅✅ [1][2]

1. Citation and context
CRASH-2 collaborators. Lancet 2010;376(9734):23-32. 274 hospitals, 40 countries. Before CRASH-2, TXA had surgical data but no large trauma trial. ✅ [1]
2. PICO





























PopulationAdults within 8 h of injury with significant bleeding or at risk (SBP below 90 and/or HR above 110, or clinician judgment) ✅ [1]InterventionTXA 1 g IV over 10 min, then 1 g IV over 8 h ✅✅ [1][2]ComparatorMatched placeboOutcomesPrimary: death in hospital within 4 weeks. Secondary: vascular occlusive events, transfusion, surgeryDesignDouble blind, placebo controlled, superiority
3. Validity: strengths and red flags

Strengths: very large, blinded, placebo controlled, simple outcome (death).
Red flags: cause of death and clot events judged by sites (misclassification likely); transfusion and surgery were similar between groups, so how it works is unclear; mostly low and middle income settings. ✅ [1]

4. Results





































OutcomeTXAPlaceboEffectARR / NNTCheckAll cause death14.5%16.0%RR 0.91 (0.85 to 0.97)1.5% / 67✅✅ [1][2]Death due to bleeding4.9%5.7%RR 0.85 (0.76 to 0.96)0.8% / 125✅✅ [1][2]Any vascular occlusive event1.7%2.0%RR 0.84 (0.68 to 1.02), not significant✅ [1]
Timing (exploratory, Roberts 2011), death due to bleeding: within 1 h RR 0.68; 1 to 3 h RR 0.79; after 3 h RR 1.44 (harm). ✅ [1]
5. Applicability at St. Mary’s
Level I trauma center: TXA belongs in the trauma bay and massive transfusion workflow, with the clock started at injury, not arrival. Ask “Did EMS already give TXA?” to avoid a duplicate load.
6. Role in therapy
“For adult trauma patients with significant bleeding, TXA 1 g over 10 minutes then 1 g over 8 hours is reasonable first line if started within 3 hours of injury; after 3 hours it is not recommended.”
7. Pharmacist’s angle

Check the time of injury before verifying.
Second gram runs over 8 hours: make sure the infusion is actually ordered.
Renal adjustment applies to repeated dosing, not the trauma load ⚠️ [VERIFY label].
Seizure risk rises with high doses ⚠️ [VERIFY].

Sources

Critical Care Reviews: CRASH-2
RCEMLearning: CRASH-2 trial
LSHTM research online: CRASH-2 paper

journal-club/jc_esett.title: JC_ESETT
journal-club/jc_esett.content:
Journal Club: ESETT (second line drugs for status epilepticus)
Key: ✅✅ two independent sources · ✅ one source · ⚠️ [VERIFY] · Template: Journal_Club_Template · Module: PICU_Core · Codes_Resuscitation
0. 60 second bottom line

“ESETT (NEJM 2019) randomized children and adults with benzodiazepine refractory convulsive status epilepticus to levetiracetam 60 mg/kg, fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg, or valproate 40 mg/kg over 10 minutes. Seizures stopped with improved responsiveness at 60 minutes in 47%, 45% and 46%: no meaningful difference. Safety was similar, with numerically more hypotension and intubation with fosphenytoin. The main limitation is early stopping and unblinding. For our ED and PICU, any of the three is acceptable second line, so pick by patient factors.” ✅✅ [1][2]

1. Citation and context
Kapur J, et al. N Engl J Med 2019 ✅ [2]. Volume and pages ⚠️ [VERIFY]. NIH funded ✅ [1]. Before ESETT, second line choice had little head to head evidence.
2. PICO

























PopulationAge 2 and older with convulsive status epilepticus despite adequate benzodiazepines; 57 US EDs ✅ [1]Intervention and comparators (all over 10 min)Levetiracetam 60 mg/kg (max 4,500 mg); fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg (max 1,500 mg PE); valproate 40 mg/kg (max 3,000 mg) ✅✅ [1][2]OutcomeSeizure cessation and improved responsiveness at 60 min without more anticonvulsantsDesignBlinded, response adaptive, stopped early for futility (384 analyzed in the three arms) ✅✅ [1][2]
3. Validity

Strengths: blinded, head to head, pragmatic ED setting.
Red flags: stopped early; 23% to 33% per group did not meet eligibility; unblinding in about half of enrollments; mixed children and adults; responsiveness is subjective ✅✅ [1][2].

4. Results















































OutcomeLevetiracetamFosphenytoinValproateCheckPrimary success47%45%46%✅✅ [1][2]Probability of being best0.410.240.35✅ [2]Life threatening hypotension0.7%3.2%1.6%✅✅ [1][2]Intubation within 60 min20%26%17%✅✅ [1][2]Death4.7%2.4%1.6%✅✅ [1][2]
5. Applicability at St. Mary’s
Children’s hospital and adult ED both apply (age 2 and up). Choose by patient: valproate avoided in pregnancy, liver disease and suspected mitochondrial disease; fosphenytoin needs cardiac monitoring; levetiracetam needs renal adjustment for maintenance.
6. Role in therapy
“For benzodiazepine refractory status epilepticus, levetiracetam, fosphenytoin or valproate are equally effective second line options; choose by patient factors.”
7. Pharmacist’s angle

Check weight and the max dose for each drug.
Fosphenytoin dosed in PE; check rate limits ⚠️ [VERIFY label].
Valproate: pregnancy, liver, and age under 2 risks.
Have the third line (anesthetic infusion) ready.

Sources

WikiJournalClub: ESETT
The Bottom Line: ESETT
NINDS press release
Full text (PMC)

journal-club/jc_ninds.title: JC_NINDS
journal-club/jc_ninds.content:
Journal Club: NINDS rt-PA Stroke Trial (alteplase within 3 hours)
Key: ✅✅ two independent sources · ✅ one source · ⚠️ [VERIFY] · Template: Journal_Club_Template · Module: Stroke_Core · Drug: Thrombolytics_Stroke
0. 60 second bottom line

“The NINDS trial (NEJM 1995) randomized 624 ischemic stroke patients within 3 hours of onset to alteplase 0.9 mg/kg (max 90 mg) or placebo. At 3 months, more alteplase patients had minimal or no disability (Barthel 95 to 100: 50% vs 38%, NNT about 8), with no difference in death. Symptomatic brain bleeding rose from 0.6% to 6.4% (NNH 17). The main limitation is fragility and baseline imbalance. For our stroke patients, this trial is why the dose, the BP limit and the clock all matter.” ✅✅ [1][2]

1. Citation and context
NINDS rt-PA Stroke Study Group. N Engl J Med 1995;333(24):1581-7. PMID 7477192. The trial that led to FDA approval of alteplase for stroke. ✅✅ [1][3]
2. PICO





























PopulationIschemic stroke, treatment within 3 h of onset (half within 90 min); long bleeding exclusion list ✅ [1]InterventionAlteplase 0.9 mg/kg, max 90 mg: 10% bolus, 90% over 60 min ✅✅ [2]Thrombolytics_StrokeComparatorPlaceboOutcomesPart 1: NIHSS improvement of 4 or more at 24 h. Part 2: global test of 4 scales at 3 monthsDesignTwo part, randomized, double blind, 8 US centers (624 total) ✅ [2]
3. Validity

Strengths: blinded, placebo controlled, patient centered 3 month outcomes.
Red flags: Part 1 primary was negative (47% vs 39%, not significant) ✅ [2]; baseline imbalance in stroke subtypes; fragility index about 3 ✅ [2] ⚠️ [VERIFY second source].

4. Results








































OutcomeAlteplasePlaceboEffectCheckFavorable global outcome at 3 monthsOR 1.7 (1.2 to 2.6)✅ [1]Barthel 95 to 10050%38%ARR 12%, NNT about 8✅ [2]Symptomatic ICH (36 h)6.4%0.6%NNH 17✅✅ [1][2]Death at 3 monthsNo significant difference✅✅ [1][2]
5. Applicability at St. Mary’s
Comprehensive stroke center: alteplase is still used, though AHA/ASA 2026 lists tenecteplase as equally preferred (see JC_AcT). The NINDS exclusions shaped today’s eligibility checklist.
6. Role in therapy
“For eligible ischemic stroke within the window, alteplase 0.9 mg/kg (max 90 mg) improves 3 month function at the cost of more symptomatic bleeding; tenecteplase is now an equal option.”
7. Pharmacist’s angle

Weigh the patient; the dose depends on it.
Waste the excess from the vial before dispensing so the full vial isn’t infused.
BP below 185/110 before, below 180/105 for 24 h after.
No antithrombotics for 24 h.

Sources

ClinCalc: NINDS brief summary
WikEM: NINDS
PubMed 7477192

Last verified: 2026-10-17.

journal-club/jc_woman.title: JC_WOMAN
journal-club/jc_woman.content:
Journal Club: WOMAN (TXA in postpartum hemorrhage)
Key: ✅✅ two independent sources · ✅ one source · ⚠️ [VERIFY] · Template: Journal_Club_Template · Module: LD_Obstetrics_Core
0. 60 second bottom line

“WOMAN (Lancet 2017) randomized about 20,000 women with postpartum hemorrhage to tranexamic acid 1 g IV (second 1 g if bleeding continued after 30 minutes) or placebo. The primary outcome, death or hysterectomy, did not differ (5.3% vs 5.5%). Death due to bleeding was lower, 1.5% vs 1.9% (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.00; NNT about 250), and the benefit was concentrated in women treated within 3 hours. The main limitation is a negative primary outcome and a fragile secondary result. For our L&D patients, TXA is an add on to uterotonics, given early.” ✅✅ [1][2]

1. Citation and context
WOMAN Trial Collaborators. Lancet 2017. ✅✅ [1][2] Volume and pages ⚠️ [VERIFY]. Partly funded by Pfizer, which makes TXA ✅ [1].
2. PICO





























PopulationWomen 16 or older with clinically diagnosed PPH (over 500 mL vaginal, over 1,000 mL cesarean, or instability) when the clinician was uncertain about TXA ✅ [1]InterventionTXA 1 g IV slowly (about 1 mL/min of 100 mg/mL); second 1 g if bleeding continued after 30 min or restarted within 24 h ✅✅ [1][2]ComparatorPlaceboOutcomesPrimary: death from any cause or hysterectomy within 42 days. Secondary: death due to bleedingDesignDouble blind, placebo controlled, 21 countries ⚠️ [VERIFY count]
3. Validity

Strengths: large, blinded, placebo controlled.
Red flags: subjective inclusion (estimated blood loss, undefined instability); sample size changed during the trial; fragility index of 0 for death due to bleeding; the discussion led with a secondary outcome ✅ [1].

4. Results















































OutcomeTXAPlaceboEffectCheckDeath or hysterectomy (primary)5.3%5.5%RR 0.97 (0.87 to 1.09), not significant✅ [1]Death due to bleeding1.5%1.9%RR 0.81 (0.65 to 1.00); NNT about 250 to 274✅✅ [1][2]Death due to bleeding, treated within 3 hRR 0.69 (0.52 to 0.91)✅ [1]; NNT 100 for 1 to 3 h ✅ [2]; arm percentages ⚠️ [VERIFY]Hysterectomy3.6%3.5%No difference✅ [1]Thromboembolic eventsNo difference✅ [1]
5. Applicability at St. Mary’s
Most deaths in WOMAN occurred in low resource settings, so the absolute benefit here is smaller. ACOG supports considering TXA when initial therapy fails. The time limit is the practical point: within 3 hours of birth.
6. Role in therapy
“For postpartum hemorrhage, TXA 1 g IV over 10 minutes, repeat once after 30 minutes if needed, is a reasonable add on to uterotonics when given within 3 hours of birth.”
7. Pharmacist’s angle

Slow IV: about 1 mL per minute (10 minutes for 1 g).
Check time of birth before verifying.
No change to the uterotonic sequence: oxytocin first; no methylergonovine with hypertension; no carboprost with asthma.

Sources

SGEM #214: WOMAN trial review
AAFP POEM: WOMAN trial
UMEM pearl: WOMAN trial

journal-club/journal_club_template.title: Journal_Club_Template
journal-club/journal_club_template.content:
Journal Club Template (trial to bedside in 60 seconds)
Use this for every trial. Fill the Bottom line last but say it first. Built from the JAMA Users’ Guides to the Medical Literature (three questions: Are the results valid? What are the results? Will they help my patients?), the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 domains, the CONSORT 2025 reporting checklist (Hopewell et al., BMJ 2025;389:e081123), and standard pharmacy residency journal club evaluation forms.

0. The 60 second bottom line (say this first)

“[Trial name] ([journal, year]) randomized [N] [population] to [intervention] vs [comparator] for [duration]. The primary outcome, [outcome], occurred in [x%] vs [y%] (ARR [z%], NNT [n]; HR [ ], 95% CI [ ]). The main limitation is [one]. For our patients at St. Mary’s, this means [practice implication].“

1. Citation and context

Citation, trial name, funding source, authors’ conflicts of interest.
Why was this trial done? What was standard care before? What gap does it fill?
Registered (ClinicalTrials.gov number)? Was the primary outcome the same as registered?

2. PICO





























PopulationKey inclusion and exclusion criteria; who was left out (pregnant, renal impairment, elderly, peds)InterventionDrug, dose, route, duration, titrationComparatorPlacebo or active? Was the comparator dosed fairly (standard of care, right dose)?OutcomesPrimary; key secondary; safetyDesignRCT, superiority vs noninferiority vs equivalence, blinding, sites, duration
3. Are the results valid? (internal validity)

































































QuestionWhat to look forRed flagRandomized properly?Method (computer, central)Alternating days, chart numbersAllocation concealed?Central or sealed opaque envelopesInvestigators could predict the next assignmentGroups similar at baseline?Table 1Big differences in severity or key risk factorsBlinded?Patients, clinicians, outcome assessorsOpen label with a subjective outcomeAnalyzed as randomized?Intention to treat (ITT) for superiorityOnly per protocol, or a “modified ITT” that drops many patientsFollow up complete?Loss to follow up and whyLosses larger than the number of events, or unequal between groupsStopped early for benefit?Planned interim analysesEarly stopping inflates effect sizePowered?Sample size calculation and assumed event rateEvent rate much lower than assumed: underpoweredPrimary outcome meaningful?Patient oriented (death, stroke, MI) vs surrogate (A1c, LDL, INR)Surrogate only; composite driven by its softest partNoninferiority trial?Margin stated and justified; both ITT and per protocol analyzedWide margin; only ITT reported (ITT biases toward noninferiority)Multiple comparisons?Prespecified secondaries and subgroupsMany subgroups, positive one highlighted
4. What are the results?

Primary outcome: events in each arm, effect size, 95% CI, p value.
Absolute risk reduction (ARR) = control event rate minus treatment event rate.
Relative risk reduction (RRR) = ARR ÷ control event rate.
NNT = 1 ÷ ARR (round up). NNH = 1 ÷ absolute risk increase for harm.
Hazard ratio / odds ratio / relative risk: below 1 favors treatment (for bad outcomes). If the 95% CI crosses 1, it is not statistically significant.
Statistical vs clinical significance: a significant p value with a tiny ARR may not change practice.
Fragility index (optional): how many patients would need a different outcome to lose significance. A small number means a fragile result.
Secondary outcomes are hypothesis generating if the primary is negative.
Safety: serious adverse events, discontinuations, deaths; who paid for the safety monitoring.

5. Will it help my patients? (external validity)

Would my patient have been enrolled? (age, kidney function, comorbidities, pregnancy, weight)
Is the comparator what we use at St. Mary’s?
Is the dose, monitoring or setting realistic here? (labs, pumps, nursing time)
Formulary, cost, availability, shortages.
What do current guidelines say, and does this trial change them?

6. Strengths and limitations (pick the top 3 of each)
7. Author’s conclusion vs your conclusion

Do the data support the authors’ wording?
Your role in therapy statement: “For [patient type], [drug] is a reasonable [first line / alternative / not recommended] because [reason].”
What further research is needed?

8. Pharmacist’s angle (always add)

Dosing, renal and hepatic adjustment, interactions, monitoring, administration.
Formulary or protocol change this could support at St. Mary’s.


Formula card

































ARRCER − EERRRRARR ÷ CERNNT1 ÷ ARRRelative riskEER ÷ CER95% CI of a ratio crossing 1Not significant95% CI of a difference crossing 0Not significant
CER = control event rate; EER = experimental event rate.
How you’ll be scored (residency style)

Accurate summary of design, methods and results.
Critique: strengths, weaknesses and their impact on the result.
Conclusion with a role in therapy and limitations.
Background knowledge: disease state and the drug’s pharmacology.
Delivery: on time, clear, answers questions.

Calculators and Drug Interactions.

st-marys/what_leadership_values.content:
What Leadership Values (and how to show it)
A pharmacist hired without residency training is often judged on three questions: Is she trained? Does she know the guidelines? Can she work alone? Answer each with evidence, not words.



































The questionWhat a resident would showWhat you will do”No residency”Structured training across rotationsThis 12 week plan, finished and documented. Keep log.md current; it is your training record.”Will she know the guidelines?”Quotes the guideline, year and recommendationEvery module page has the source and year. Drill the “quote it” lines.”Can she work alone on nights?”Safe, independent verification; knows when to escalateCodes, trauma and stroke modules come early. Know who to call for each service.”Will she fit in?”Easy to work with, reliable, asks good questionsTake hard shifts, close the loop on every call, thank the techs.”Will she stay current?”CE, journal club, safety alertsISMP and FDA weekly; one CE event per quarter.
What hospital pharmacy leaders are measured on

Medication errors and adverse drug events (and catching them before they reach the patient).
Turnaround time for STAT and first doses.
Joint Commission readiness: high alert drug processes, look alike sound alike, compounding compliance.
Drug cost and waste; drug shortages.
Antimicrobial stewardship metrics.

When you say something in a huddle or a call, tie it to one of these.
Relationships

After your first weeks, show the pharmacy leaders one module and one case you worked through. Ask one specific question, not a general one.
A short note at 30 and 90 days on what you completed (modules, interventions, inservice) shows the residency equivalent in writing.

Verify locally at St. Mary’s

Who covers NICU and PICU verification on nights?
Is there a pediatric or neonatal clinical pharmacist, and when are they on?
Where are the order sets, protocols and policies kept (intranet, Lexicomp, Cerner)?
